#5744. Southern Co. eyes $100B spending plan on natural gas, nuclear and other investments

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Executives downplayed the potential for sweeping political change to impact the company’s strategy and growth plans. “I feel pretty confident about what we have in place,” CEO Chris Womack said.

Southern Co. could see its five-year capital plan increase to $100 billion on natural gas investments, nuclear uprates and additional generation, executives told investors and analysts during a third-quarter earnings call last week.

They also downplayed the potential for sweeping political change following the midterm elections to impact the company’s strategy, particularly with regards to large-load customers like data centers that are fueling its growth plans. Anger over energy costs, including electricity bills, helped Democrats seize control of Congress and many state leadership positions, including in Georgia, where they won the governor’s office and a majority on the Public Service Commission.

“I feel pretty confident about what we have in place,” CEO Chris Womack said.

He said he has not heard “any talk about retroactive” data center freezes or “looking backwards” at signed contracts.

“We have strong confidence in ... what we've done in the contracts that we signed that are in place and are in effect,” Womack said.

David Poroch, the company’s executive vice president and CFO, said even if development slows down and data centers don’t ramp as quickly as expected, its contracts contain provisions for minimum bills that cover at least 100% of the cost being introduced into the system.

“Before the kilowatt moves over the meter, we are recovering our costs embedded in those minimum bills,” Poroch said. “So we've kind of disengaged ourselves from the need for a customer to achieve their ramp rate for us to recover our cost.”

Womack also listed several large loads that are not data centers, which he said will continue to fuel economic growth in the South, including projects from Airbus, Mitsubishi Power, Audi and others. Mitsubishi Power plans to greatly expand its gas turbine manufacturing facility in Savannah, Georgia, helping meet rising power generation needs, he said.

The company added about $4 billion to the $81 billion base capital plan the company rolled out in February. The additions include 400 MW of uprates at existing natural gas facilities and an expansion of the Southeast Connector gas pipeline.

In the third quarter, the company's Georgia Power subsidiary also received approval for an agreement with Google to expand nuclear capacity through uprates over the next several years, said Poroch. The company is also bidding on new generation contracts in Alabama and Georgia, he added.

“To the extent potential company-owned resources are selected through these processes and ultimately authorized by the respective [regulators], this could represent substantial incremental investment, together with opportunities for additional investment across all our businesses,” Poroch said.

In response to an analyst’s question, he said he expects more than 90% of new investment to target state-regulated projects versus competitive power markets and interstate pipelines.

In the third quarter of 2026, retail electric revenues were $6.6 billion compared to $5.7 billion for the corresponding period in 2025, and $16 billion year to date compared to $15.1 billion in 2025, according to its quarterly filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company attributed the increase to changes in rates and pricing, and higher contributions from commercial and industrial customers.

Southern saw weather-normalized electricity sales across all customer segments rise 3.5% in the third quarter and 2.7% year to date, led by commercial sales, which were up 7.3% compared with the third quarter of 2025.

“This large load customer demand is translating into increasing usage,” Womack said. “Notably, data center usage was 59% higher this quarter and is now up 52% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from data center customers.”

He said the company’s portfolio of signed large-load contracts has grown to 21 GW with an additional 7 GW in late stages across Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi.

“Now, are we going to land 75 GW of projects? Probably not,” said Womack, referring to the company’s speculative pipeline. “I mean, we'll continue to risk adjust it, but I think it's a clear indication and a demonstration of the interest in our territory.”

#5743. 300 Glaciers Have Disappeared from the American West Since the Mid‑20th Century — the Survivors Have a Few Things in Common

From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.

A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared, way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise. Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.

When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.

We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).

I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.

The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.

We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.

It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states.

In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.

In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.

The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.

The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems. The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.

While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production.

An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.

High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat.

The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.

By Andrew Fountain, Professor of Geography, Portland State University

#5742. Outer Spaces takes solar beyond the rooftop with integrated backyard energy system

Residential solar is finding a new place to call home: the backyard.

Outer Spaces, a new company founded by the entrepreneurs behind outdoor living brand Outer, is introducing a solar-powered pavilion that combines photovoltaic generation, battery storage and usable outdoor living space. The company’s first product, OS1, can be designed for multiple functions, including an outdoor kitchen, office, gym or gathering space, while generating electricity and providing backup power for the home.

Outer Spaces is planning to produce outdoor structures that integrate solar PV and energy storage. Credit: Outer Spaces

The California-based company is positioning OS1 as a new category of residential energy infrastructure that goes beyond conventional rooftop arrays and garage-mounted batteries. It builds on the growing interest in solar structures that also serve a secondary purpose.

OS1 combines a solar pavilion with a finished outdoor power deck. Solar panels integrated into the overhead structure generate electricity, while a thin battery storage system is housed beneath the deck. According to Outer Spaces, the combination allows the structure to produce energy throughout the day and provide backup power during outages.

Rather than competing exclusively with traditional rooftop solar, OS1 offers homeowners an additional way to use available property for energy production, particularly when roof aesthetics, space limitations, or homeowner preferences become obstacles to conventional installations.

Outer Spaces describes OS1 as a modular system designed for rapid on-site assembly, with minimal to no excavation required. The company says installation avoids traditional construction steps such as concrete pouring and lumber cutting. Once the structure is assembled, a licensed electrician then connects its energy system to the customer’s home.

The product’s first availability is scheduled for 2027, beginning in Southern California and select additional markets; pricing is expected to be announced in early 2027.

Solar canopies and pergolas have increasingly incorporated features such as EV charging, lighting, fans and weather protection, giving homeowners additional reasons to invest in solar outside the traditional rooftop model.

Outer Spaces represents another potential avenue for expanding residential solar adoption through design-driven products. The opportunity will ultimately depend on pricing, installation economics, permitting requirements and the system’s measurable energy performance.

Outer Spaces plans to showcase OS1 publicly for the first time at RE+ 2026, Nov. 16 to 19, in Las Vegas.

#5741. What’s next for California’s climate laws following an appeals court split decision

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals allowed Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions reporting under SB 253 to move forward while halting the enforcement of scope 3 reporting and SB 261.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals issued a split decision on California’s climate disclosure laws, Senate Bill 253 and Senate Bill 261, on Monday, allowing some emissions reporting requirements to proceed, while blocking others on the basis of them being considered in part or completely unconstitutional under the First Amendment.

In the decision, the federal appellate panel partially upheld and partially overturned a district court's decision from August 2025, which declined to enjoin the laws. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business associations filed the lawsuit, requesting to temporarily block implementation of both climate laws while their constitutionality was under review.

Implementation of SB 261 was already temporarily halted pending review by the Ninth Circuit last November.

SB 253, or the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act, requires companies with more than $1 billion in revenue to report Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, with eventual Scope 3 disclosures. SB 261, or the Climate-Related Financial Risk Act, requires companies with more than $500 million in revenue to publicly disclose their climate-related financial risks and countermeasures. Both climate disclosure regulations were signed into law in October 2023 by California Gov. Gavin Newsom and have since faced a spate of legal challenges.

The ruling came a day before the inaugural emissions disclosure deadline for SB 253.

The Nov. 9 decision allowed for the reporting of a company’s direct emissions to proceed under SB 253’s Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosure requirements, affirming the lower court’s decision. The court ruled such disclosures “regulate commercial speech,” which the appellate panel defined as factual and objective information on a company’s own operations.

However, the appeals court reversed the lower court’s ruling when it came to SB 253’s Scope 3 disclosure requirements, which ask companies to report the indirect emissions generated from their supply chain. The appellate panel said Scope 3 reporting requirements outlined under the bill were considered “likely unconstitutional” as they demanded supply chain data that was “insufficiently tethered” to a company’s own operations and, hence, failed to qualify as commercial speech.

The majority of the appellate panel also concluded that SB 261 “compels noncommercial speech” by requiring covered companies to disclose their financial exposure to climate change risks in biennial reports based on the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework.

U.S. Circuit Judge Jacqueline Nguyen wrote in the Nov. 9 opinion that this requirement asks companies to publish “value-laden judgments on a politically fraught subject” that “go beyond providing economic information tethered to any commercial transaction.”

Nguyen said disclosures demanded under SB 261 ran afoul of First Amendment protections and were likely unconstitutional, ruling the law cannot be enforced. The federal judge added that the state of California could have relied on less restrictive measures to achieve its goals, such as asking for voluntary climate-related financial risk disclosures.

The court’s decision came a day before companies subject to SB 253 were required to submit their first annual Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for the most recent fiscal year to the California Air Resources Board, the agency tasked with enforcing the state’s climate risk disclosure rules

CARB’s website still states Nov. 10 to be the reporting deadline for covered companies and, since the Ninth Circuit did not pause enforcement of Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting, the deadline remained legally active. The agency has yet to release an official summary tallying submission counts from this week.

“The principal question facing companies will be whether and when to devote resources to SB 253 Scope 1 and 2 compliance,” Ropes & Gray attorneys Michael Littenberg, Marc Rotter and Peter Witschi wrote in a Tuesday post. “CARB’s various reporting accommodations for this year effectively turned fiscal 2025 compliance into a practice run. Based on CARB’s pre-rulemaking proposals, SB 253 Scope 1 and 2 compliance will ratchet up next year, with more prescriptive disclosure requirements and limited assurance kicking in.”

However, the attorneys noted that the prediction is based on the assumption that Scope 1 and 2 reporting survives going forward and there are “no other intervening developments that delay or modify that portion of SB 253 for next year.”

The Ropes & Gray attorneys said pausing compliance work on indirect emissions, or Scope 3 reporting, seems to be a “low-risk proposition,” given the Ninth Circuit’s decision. The law firm also noted that given CARB’s reporting requirements under SB 253 for 2027 onwards are still in the early drafting stages, companies still lack guidance on what they would need to do to comply in the future.

At this time, the fate of SB 261 seems most uncertain. The Ninth Circuit of Appeals temporarily paused enforcement of the law last November after the Chamber of Commerce and other business groups filed an emergency application with the U.S. Supreme Court to block both climate laws pending the outcome of their appeal filed in the appellate court. Though the group requested that the implementation of both climate disclosure laws be halted, the Ninth Circuit only granted the motion for injunction pending appeal to the enforcement of SB 261.

Given the status of the law, experts from law firm Morrison & Foerster said it is “unlikely that companies will have to comply with SB 261’s reporting requirements in the near future.” However, the firm noted that companies should continue to monitor the trial court proceedings.

Law firm Crowell & Moring echoed this guidance in a Monday post analyzing the Ninth Circuit’s split decision.

“The decision supports preliminary relief for SB 261 and Scope 3 but should not be described as permanently striking down those requirements,” the firm wrote. “Companies should monitor the mandate, district court proceedings and implementing injunction orders, CARB’s response, and any requests for rehearing or further review to evaluate future compliance activities.”

#5740. Democrats Are at COP31 to Show That the US Has Not Abandoned the Fight Against Climate Change

The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 COP conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.

Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at COP is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the COP31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend COP summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.

Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at COP nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at COP with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

By Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex

“The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (CVOW) is essential for American national security and meeting Virginia’s dramatically growing energy needs, the fastest growth in America. This growth is driven by the need to provide reliable power to many of America’s most important war fighting installations, the world’s largest warship manufacturer, and the largest concentration of data centers on the planet as well as the leading edge of the AI revolution.

These electrons will power the data centers that will win the AI race, support our war fighters, and build the nuclear warships needed to maintain our maritime supremacy. #5738. The Trump Administration’s Pro-Cancer Agenda

Under Trump, Americans could face an extraordinary increase in exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

Over the nearly two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, his administration has taken more than 500 actions that harm public health or the environment. When faced with this onslaught of harm, it can be difficult to see the strategic agenda at play. However, NRDC’s new analysis reveals that the Trump administration is executing a sweeping and long planned—but quiet—government-wide campaign to dismember major programs that are intended to prevent exposure to cancer-causing toxics and radiation. In sum, this administration has reversed course: America’s government is no longer fighting a “War on Cancer” but fighting a “War to Promote Cancer.”

This is not an accident. Much of this campaign can be found throughout the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 blueprint and has long been advocated for by industry. But a healthy life should not be treated as an obstacle to somebody else’s profit margin. The freedom to breathe clean air, drink safe water, eat safe food, work without needless exposure to carcinogens, and raise children without avoidable toxic risks should be among the most basic expectations of life in America. Americans should not have to wonder whether the water coming from their taps contains cancer-causing chemicals, whether the air they breathe carries toxic pollution from a nearby industrial facility, or whether going to work means being unnecessarily exposed to carcinogens.

Instead of ensuring these basic freedoms, the Trump administration is creating a system in which polluters are given greater leeway to expose everyone in the nation to cancer-causing toxics and radiation.

#5737. Utility, tech officials see opportunities to increase grid utilization

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Specialized AI models and grid-enhancing technologies could help, but the industry already has the basic planning and tools to make the grid more flexible, panelists said at the BNEF Houston Summit.

The panel on grid utilization was held as utilities, hyperscalers and regulators are scrambling to accommodate large-load demand amid backlash from ratepayers concerned about affordability.

Grid Strategies, a consultancy that publishes a closely-watched annual report on U.S. bulk power supply and demand, said late last year that the systemwide load factor is about 60%, heading to 66% by 2030. Grid Strategies defines load factor as the ratio of average energy usage to peak load.

Some utilities run their systems at even lower load factors.

In response to a first-of-its-kind legislative mandate, Dominion Energy’s Virginia subsidiary revealed last month that its distribution grid runs at an average load factor of 41% and peaks just under 80% utilization. Its transmission system’s “median facility utilization” is about 33%, though individual facilities may approach or exceed rated capacity during outages, demand peaks or “significant power transfers,” Dominion said.

Jessica Hogle, NRG’s vice president of federal affairs, said that utilities should think ambitiously about grid flexibility.

“We should just say: ‘This is our goal and we will get there’,” Hogle said.

NRG, a Texas-based independent power producer and retail energy provider, aims to deliver 25 GW of demand response, energy storage and virtual power plant capacity by 2035, she said, adding that NRG believed the goal was ambitious but achievable.

Hogle joined NRG in June. She began her career in the electricity business with Pacific Gas & Electric Corp. as the San Francisco-based investor-owned utility navigated shifting policy winds, she said.

“We would say, there is no way we could do this in terms of integrating these resources, it is too hard and too expensive,” Hogle said, paraphrasing the company’s message to California legislators mulling ever-stricter renewable energy mandates.

In the end, PG&E’s concerns were overblown, she said, adding: “We exceeded the targets.”

California’s power-sector emissions fell significantly as its renewable generation share grew.

Getting more out of the existing grid — finding “a better way to optimize every dollar” — could likewise have broad-based economic and societal benefits, said Arushi Sharma Frank, a Texas-based energy consultant and strategic advisor to the Utilize Coalition.

“The AI narrative is very important, but underneath that, there is [the] onshoring of everything we need,” she said, referring to efforts to site more heavy and high-tech manufacturing in the United States. “We can’t do any of that if we operate in the same mindset we’ve had for years.”

Grid operators already use tools to improve grid flexibility and increase headroom, like the Remedial Action Schemes common in the Western Interconnection, said Dave Berry, CEO of “powered land” developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure.

A Remedial Action Scheme is, in essence, a logic pathway that defines how the grid responds to a disturbance such as a line or generator outage, Berry said. The drawback is that by curtailing generation or load to protect customers in one area, a RAS may harm their counterparts in another.

“The challenge is getting all the stakeholders aligned,” Berry said.

Sharma Frank, an advisor to the data center flexibility startup Emerald AI, predicted more software-based flexibility solutions too.

Inside utilities, artificial intelligence tools can break down silos between grid planners and operators that have both been hamstrung in different ways by constraints on analytical capacity, she said.

“That is the other interesting part about the AI boom: We have compute that we didn’t have before,” Sharma Frank said. “This unlocks the ability to see [grid] capacity that we didn’t see before.”

#5736. To Honor Veterans, How About We Stop The Oil Wars?

Today is Veterans Day in the United States. Naturally, across the country, people have spent at least part of the day thinking about veterans they know as well as veterans they don’t and thanking them for their service. Whether you agree with the various wars the United States has gotten into or not, you have to honor and appreciate the human beings who offered to put their lives on the line in order to support their country (or think that they’re doing so, at least). I know several people who are veterans, and they typically sacrificed a lot in their previous military roles.

However, I do have to come back to the rationale for the wars we as a country get into. I’m 44 years old, and it seems like we’ve been involved in wars related to oil and gas for more than half of my life. It’s just a continual process. We get into a war in the Middle East connected to XYZ, but it’s really about oil. After years of over-involvement, destruction, and death, society realizes it’s been a super counterproductive, idiotic war and we pull out. The, after a few years, we begin again and the story repeats.

Well, how about we just stop getting involved in oil wars? How about we stop depending so much on oil supply from foreign nations and global oil markets? How about we respect our countrymen and countrywomen who sign up to serve by not sending them into pointless forever wars in the Middle East to get traumatized, injured, or killed? That would be truly honoring veterans of the past as well as protecting current and future Americans.

#5735. Secure Solar Futures set to install 313-kW array on Virginia elementary school

Secure Solar Futures, a commercial solar contractor, will build a 313-kW solar power system at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, Virginia. Construction of the system is expected to start later this year at no cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year power purchase agreement with Secure Solar Futures.

A total of 531 bifacial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, Texas, will be installed on the rooftop of the school, and the array is expected to offset 67% of the power used by the school annually. In its first year, the school’s solar system is projected to produce 421 MWh of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes.

Under the PPA, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy and Secure Solar Futures will own, operate and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

Preston Park Elementary School is expected to save $581,000 electricity costs over the term of the PPA. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s lifespan.

#5734. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. Initial reports following Democrats' huge midterm win earlier this month made it sound like Donald Trump had lost his will to continue fighting Republicans' war with Iran. Before the midterms, Trump talked constantly about raining down fire from heaven as soon as Republicans won, but his attitude reportedly changed after losing both the House and the Senate. With hopes of a peace deal revived, oil prices fell, but Trump can't stop being Trump. He's since sent oil prices back up after claiming the U.S. doesn't actually need to make a deal with Iran anymore.

Posting on TruthSocial at about 8:00 a.m., Trump wrote, "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT." It's been a long time since you could trust anything Trump says, but it sure sounds like his idea of giving up without giving up is for the Navy to continue blockading the Strait of Hormuz, even if it's costing us a fortune.

The cost of operating that blockade — a blockade that we didn't need before Republicans started this disastrous war, by the way — is reportedly somewhere around $14 billion a year. Of course, what says "Art of the Deal" quite like paying billions for something you used to get for free? That's just Trump's style, baby. But you can also see the appeal of trying to maintain the status quo as long as possible, since actually fixing this mess appears to be more than Republicans can handle, but escalating the violence is now even less practical than it was before. For some reason, the oil traders didn't like that.

At the time of writing, Brent Crude prices were up 2.6% for the day, rising to $95.10 a barrel. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate is trading at $88.16 a barrel, up 1.9% for the day. Those certainly aren't the highest prices we've seen recently, but pricier oil isn't great news for fuel prices, either. The oil traders definitely don't like hearing Trump say he plans to waste $14 billion a year in taxpayer dollars, just to continue operating the blockade that still won't win the war.

Still, there may be another issue shaking oil traders' confidence in the likelihood of a peace deal. While Trump isn't known for his grasp of the details, he also does a terrible job of staying focused, and that post about not needing a deal with Iran didn't just talk about Iran. Trump actually started his old-man rantings by saying his main focus between now and January is political retribution:

I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S. The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters. Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month. Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!

If you've been paying attention to who Trump is and how he operates at any point in the last decade, terrorizing states that didn't vote for him makes way more sense than those wishcasting editorials about how Trump may finally work with Democrats to turn things around. If he's focused on punishing his perceived political enemies, that's time he can't spend focused on negotiating an actual peace deal with Iran. After all, he only has so much time between golfing, taking naps during meetings, and frequent doctor's appointments. Will we see oil cross the $100 mark again in the next few months? That remains to be seen and unfortunately depends on the whims of a man whose brain has almost completely turned to soup.

#5732. The High-Rise Bottleneck: Why EV Charging in Indian Apartments Is an Engineering Puzzle

Most Western clean-energy reporting takes a very specific picture of home charging for granted. You pull into a private driveway, plug into an attached garage wall-box, and pull cheap power while you sleep.

That reality does not exist for most urban drivers in India.

Data from Kazam and the Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (AEEE) shows that roughly 70% to 75% of urban households in major Indian metros live in multi-family apartments and cooperative housing societies. Parking means an open ground level slot or a space two levels down in a concrete basement. When someone here buys an electric car, their biggest hurdle isn’t battery degradation or highway chargers. It’s their own building.

As an electrical engineer in India, I watch this play out every week. Someone buys an EV, assumes they can hire a local wireman to pull power from their flat’s meter to their parking bay, and runs straight into transformer limits, cable physics, and nervous managing committees.

Here is what is actually going on beneath the floorboards.

Indian housing societies buy electricity under a bulk “sanctioned load” from their local utility (DISCOM). The utility sizes the local transformer using an electrical diversity factor the simple assumption that not all 100 flats will run their air conditioners, geysers, and induction stoves at the exact same moment.

A domestic geyser pulls 2 kW for ten minutes and shuts off. A 7.4 kW AC wall-box pulls 32 amps continuously for six to eight hours. When several residents plug in around 8:00 PM, that heavy, unbroken draw lands on the transformer right as domestic air conditioning and kitchen loads hit their evening peak.

Let’s look at the numbers on a 100-flat complex running on a standard 250 kVA transformer:

Here is where the grid cracks: just five or six cars charging at 7.4 kW pull 37 kW to 44 kW. That wipes out the 30 kW buffer completely. If eight cars plug in at once (59.2 kW), the transformer goes straight into thermal overload.

When that happens, the main incomer breaker trips plunging common areas and elevators into darkness or the utility slaps the society with massive Maximum Demand penalties on their next power bill. Getting a utility to upgrade a transformer or approve higher sanctioned load requires significant capital, transformer yard space, and months of red tape.

In a detached house, wiring an EV charger means running 5 or 10 metres of cable from your distribution board to the garage.

In an Indian high-rise, your electricity meter sits in a ground-floor panel room or inside a service shaft on the 14th floor. Your car is parked two floors beneath the earth in Basement 2. Connecting the two is an expensive engineering problem:

Even if an owner is willing to foot the entire wiring bill, they still need a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from their housing society committee or Resident Welfare Association (RWA).

Most RWA committees are volunteer residents without technical backgrounds. When handed a request for high-power continuous charging, their hesitation usually comes down to three worries:

The courts are starting to step in. In Amit Dholakia v. The State of Maharashtra (2025), the Bombay High Court pushed state authorities to issue clear guidelines preventing arbitrary NOC rejections. More recently, in early 2026, the Supreme Court of India issued notice on a Public Interest Litigation challenging arbitrary charger bans across states. While the legal momentum is clearly moving toward protecting a resident’s right to charge, taking a court ruling to a heated Sunday morning society meeting rarely makes for a quick installation.

Treating an electric car like an extra microwave where everyone pulls their own line from their domestic meter does not scale. Societies have to build shared electrical infrastructure.

India’s EV transition is moving fast on two and three wheels. But passenger electric cars won’t reach mass adoption until high-rises solve the overnight charging puzzle.

The vehicles are ready, and buyers want them. But until building codes, dynamic load balancing, and society committees catch up with automotive engineering, the hardest part of driving electric in India will simply be charging at home.

#5730. That Mystery SUV Spied In Moab Is An Audi-Bodied Test Mule For The New Scouts

A few days ago, Reddit user CapnDangerPony took to the r/whatisthiscar subreddit with a far-away photo of a very strange-looking test mule driving around in Moab. The poster only got a good photo of the side of the mule, and another from further away that gave a glimpse of its front end, neither of which revealed any details aside from a strange shape, lots of camouflage, and some sort of body-on-frame platform. Now our spies have gotten a better look at the test mule, and I know exactly what it is: This is an early prototype for the new Scouts.

Somehow, I don't think I saw a single comment online thinking that it was a Scout mule based on the Reddit photos, but that's definitely what it is. This time, it wasn't spied in Moab but at a secret Audi test facility in Germany, which is one of the few giveaways as to its identity — another obvious one being the tow hooks. I've already been surprised that Scout test mules haven't been regularly spied by now, since just this week Scout announced that it's starting to construct "validation builds" at its factory in newly blue South Carolina, and prototypes with closer-to-production bodies have apparently already been out there for months. This one is likely an older mule that's still out there racking up test miles, which is probably fine since since the Scouts have been delayed so much.

So, all of you distraught internet commenters can rest easy now. The mystery is solved. This weird test mule is for the Scout Terra and Traveler — my guess is the Traveler because of its shorter wheelbase — and despite how strange it looks, there's still some information we can glean from it.

There have been persistent rumors that Audi wants to build a competitor for the Mercedes-Benz G-Class using a modified version of the Scout's platform (and at the same factory), which seems to be at least partially why Volkswagen wanted to resurrect the brand at all, and could also be a reason for some of the trucks' delays and development problems. Audi has yet to green-light that project, so it's highly unlikely this mule is testing out a new Audi model, but the company is clearly helping out with the vehicle's engineering.

It is wearing an Audi body, though, specifically one from a Q6 E-Tron. It's basically just a placeholder, so Scout can test out the platform and powertrain without needing to put a real design on top yet. It's got huge fender flares tacked on, and you can see that the wheelbase is longer than the Q6's, with the wheels sitting in cut-outs made in the wheel arches. There's clearly a big battery pack under there, with rudimentary side steps added on in a similar fashion to the GMC Hummer EV, and the chunky six-lug wheels wear BFGoodrich all-terrain tires.

The rear tow hooks are just likes the ones on the Scout show trucks, as are the overall shapes of the bumpers, and the bits we can see of this mule's suspension setup appear to align with what Scout has shown us of its architecture. There's no tells as to whether this test mule is running the fully electric setup or is the range-extender hybrid model that will use a four-cylinder Volkswagen engine behind the rear axle; it's likely the latter, as the vast majority of Scout reservations have been for the EREV, and Scout will start production with them.

Scout first broke ground on its plant in Blythewood, South Carolina, two and a half years ago, with the project being part of a $2 billion investment that hopes to create more than 4,000 jobs. Now the company says it's starting early validation builds "to validate vehicle engineering, buildability and parts maturity while confirming that newly installed equipment is set up and functioning as expected." The company has started welding, assembly and painting operations, and in the background of a released photo we can see a couple bodies-in-white of the Traveler SUV.

750 robots help to put together 160 individual parts using 5,000 weld points, and don't worry, there's "AI-supported weld monitoring" so that everything is perfect. An "advanced metrology system" is also used to match the body against the engineering specs, checking thousands of measurements. Scout says the body shop can process up to 40 vehicles per hour, but right now the company is just testing things to make sure it all works properly before real manufacturing starts. Next it's sent through "an electrified automotive paint shop" before the truck goes to assembly, where the painted body is attached to the chassis and humans put all the components together.

The company says "validation vehicle builds will continue and mature into 2027 as Scout Motors prepares for its next phase of pre-production vehicle builds. As engineering, buildability and parts maturity advance, the manufacturing team will progress from equipment set up and functionality to proving manufacturing processes and ultimately scaling those processes toward production speed." There's no word as to updated production timelines beyond that, apart from Scout saying first deliveries are planned to start "in 2028." According to MotorTrend, the company has 210,000 pre-orders with that number expected to increase to 400,000, or about 12 to 18 months of confirmed sales, and executives deny any further delays.

#5729. SOLRITE and sonnen collaborate on integrated VPP breaker

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

#5728. Doctor Behind Mass Shooting in D.C., Police Say

— Emergency physician accused of shooting multiple people -- one fatally -- before killing himself

Emergency physician Matt Lambert, MD, was named by NBC News as the gunman in Thursday's mass shooting in Washington, D.C., citing law enforcement officials.

According to police, Lambert fatally shot a man at a gym and left another in critical condition before fleeing and shooting others. He then killed himself after barricading himself in an apartment.

Lambert described himself on his website as a clinician and entrepreneur. Lambert holds active medical licenses in West Virginia and Montana, according to DocInfo.org. Neither license lists any disciplinary action.

An X account that appears to be associated with Lambert posted a manifesto on Thursday morning, which included a screenshot of a document with Lambert's name on it.

"My manifesto is an engineering report," the post stated. Police had said earlier in the day their suspect apparently had a dispute with the building's homeowners association.

The X account, OfMiceandMold, hosts dozens of images and complaints about problems with the condo and building. Lambert's name is mentioned several times in documents or screenshots of documents, including a lawsuit in which Lambert is the plaintiff.

The address on Lambert's website is on 15th Street, where the shooting occurred.

The shootings occurred around 8 a.m. in Logan Circle, about a mile north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street Northwest was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke's Episcopal Church, residences, and a Whole Foods supermarket. Schools were locked down.

Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building and on the ground below.

Witness James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there around 8 a.m. when the shooting began.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Spellman said he and others dashed out of the gym. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

Officials believe Lambert shot another person in a parking garage elevator, and then barricaded himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said.

Another witness, Ryan Dubicki, said he was in his nearby apartment around the same time when he "heard about five bangs."

"They were really spread out so I thought it was construction," he said. A short time later, "there were cops everywhere."

The Logan Circle neighborhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the neighborhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.

Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today.

#5727. BYD Is Combining Solar Energy Storage, Five-Minute Flash Charging, And Robotic Arms For Its New Charging Stations

Despite not selling any cars in the U.S., China's BYD is quietly taking over the EV world. It has surpassed Tesla as the world's largest electric carmaker by global sales, and it's also been hard at work trying to dethrone Tesla as the provider of the world's most advanced EV charging network. Now it's announced the latest big step toward that goal. On Tuesday, BYD announced that it will combine clean solar power, its proprietary Flash Charging tech that uses local energy storage, and robotic arms into one EV charging system.

The core of this system is BYD's Flash Charging, which draws power from the grid like any other EV charging station. Unlike others, though, it stores the electricity in two on-site 185-kilowatt batteries. That stored energy can then be pumped into your EV way quicker than it would be if it were drawing from the grid directly, BYD says.

Each Flash Charger has two connectors, capable of up to 1,500 kW charging if only one is in use, or 1,000 kW if two cars are sharing. For context, Tesla's new V4 Superchargers top out at 500 kW, regular superchargers hit 250 kW, and the fastest DC chargers from Electrify America can do 350 kW. BYD's quoted charge times are 10% to 70% in five minutes, 10% to 97% in nine minutes, and in cold weather, 20% to 97% in 12 minutes given an ambient temperature of minus 30 degrees Fahrenheit.

BYD is now incorporating solar generation into the equation, drawing power from the sun to those same local 185-kW batteries, presumably via solar panels placed on top of the charging station's canopy. This means the system is less reliant on the grid, which is huge in remote, sun-soaked regions like, say, the desert in the United Arab Emirates where BYD launched all this.

Then there are the robotic arms. The idea is far from new or original — Tesla promised them a decade ago, and EV makers like Volkswagen, Hyundai, and China's Xiaomi have since built their own renditions. It's a simple premise: A robotic arm locates your car's charging port, opens the cover, and inserts the connector automatically.

BYD plans to install 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of next year. Don't expect all or even most of them to get solar power or the robot arms initially, but if BYD can actually normalize five-minute charging with solar and robot arms sometime in the next couple of years, we might be looking at the new charging network king.

#5725. 1970 Buick Wildcat For Sale With 31,908 Miles Shown Offers 455 V8 With One-Owner History

Some cars don't do small. Or economical. They're big-block-toting, street-sailing cruise ships with little regard for petite parking spaces. Tight garages need not apply. That's exactly where the Buick Wildcat lives. At almost 18 and a half feet long, a 1970 Wildcat fits the land yacht bill, though it doesn't fit into many other places. It's a testament to the automotive excess of the era, right down to its huge, 455-cubic-inch V8. Make no mention of how the average MPG in the '70s compares to today. Still, even in a time when efficiency is important to the average car buyer, collectors and enthusiasts want the big ol' boats. If that describes you, this surviving B-body muscle cruiser is up for grabs.

This 1970 Buick Wildcat is clean, too. Original paint? Check. Factory interior? Also yes. Heck, the seller says this big cat has belonged to the same owner since they bought it new over half a century ago. Of course, you might expect a 56-year-old car to have some serious mileage on its clock. Not this one. It's listed in Mount Clemens, Michigan, with just 31,908 original miles. If you've got the garage space, this old Buick needs a driver to rack up some mileage.

What's not to love? First off, it's called the "Wildcat." Certainly cool enough to land Buick on the list of automakers that have the coolest model names, according to our readers. This one, posted for sale by Michael's Auto Sales in Mount Clemens, Michigan, is something of a time capsule. The 1970 Buick Wildcat wears the original Sherwood Green Iridescent shade, along with a similarly verdant original interior. The original seats and interior treatments survived the years, right down to the door sills and green factory Buick carpeting. Even the climate control selector and radio are delightfully original. Speaking of climate control, this one has air conditioning, an option you could have selected from the factory back in 1970.

Then there's the lump under the hood. It's a 455-cubic-inch, naturally aspirated big block V8. That's eight cylinders and 7.4 liters of displacement. Displacement so cavernous, in fact, it puts the Buick's 455-cubic-inch mill among the biggest V8 engines ever put into production cars. That engine, a first for the Le Sabre-based 1970 Wildcat, had a factory horsepower rating of 370. Doesn't sound like a lot for such a massive V8, but it also produced a stump-pulling 510 pound-feet of torque.

Don't go thinking you're going to find a manual gearbox with which to row that behemoth 455-cubic-inch V8, though. This one sports a three-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatic transmission. Don't expect an immaculate, concours-condition car, either. For instance, there's a little damage on the hood breaking up the expanses of Sherwood Green Iridescent paintwork. If anything, this Wildcat is a solid, well-preserved driver. It does, however, come with original documentation, including a detailed ownership history.

As of this writing, the Wildcat is up for sale for $29,995. Not too shabby for a big-body American muscle cruiser, especially one in this condition. It is a bit pricier than the average Wildcat of this vintage, though. Hagerty puts the average 1970 Buick in excellent condition at about $12,833. And that's the high end of the value range. Drop down to an example in good condition, and that average value drops to $8,367 on the high side. Still, your average 56-year-old Wildcat isn't likely to have a mileage this low.

A 1970 Buick Wildcat convertible, on the other hand, is worth a bit more. A ragtop in excellent condition is closer to $32,700. A drop top in good condition drops things down to around $21,633 on the high side of the value range.

It is rare that a 1970 Buick Wildcat like this one would live its many years without updates and modifications? Definitely, but it's much wilder that this big ol' classic cat has such a low odometer reading. It's true; this one-owner Wildcat shows just 31,908 miles – every one of which the seller says are original. That's an average of less than 570 miles per year. Somebody, please drive this big green B-body; it's waited long enough.

#5724. Senators Investigate Whether RFK Jr. Lied to Congress About Samoa Trip

— HHS has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines"

Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after the Associated Press and the Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony.

The new inquiry is one of a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate from Republicans in the midterm elections.

Sens. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) said in a letter Wednesday to Children's Health Defense (CHD), a nonprofit group known for anti-vaccine activism that was formerly chaired by Kennedy, that they were starting an investigation.

The lawmakers asked the group for a broad range of documents related to Kennedy's Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign, and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also requested all communications between the group and federal government officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025.

AP and Guardian reporting in August showed that while Kennedy repeatedly told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation last year that his visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had "nothing to do with vaccines," a letter he sent to the Samoan prime minister ahead of the trip on CHD letterhead showed otherwise. In the letter, Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times.

"We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children," Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. "We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate's ability to fulfill its constitutional duties."

HHS has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines." In response to an AP inquiry in August, it said "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory."

Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted.

Kennedy's Samoa visit has become one of the most contentious events in his career. At the time, he was leading CHD. Critics said the visit fueled anti-vaccine sentiment in Samoa, which later experienced the measles outbreak that killed 83 people, mostly children under 5.

In the letter reported by the AP and Guardian, dated Jan. 20, 2019, Kennedy addressed then-Prime Minister Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi and described his desire to study Samoa's use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

Kennedy speculated that the deaths in Samoa may have been caused by issues with different vaccine lots. Writing on CHD letterhead, he said his team wanted to evaluate whether that was the case through a "detailed health informatics assessment."

He expressed his belief that it was difficult and time-consuming in most of the world to investigate "adverse health events associated with vaccines" and said health information systems are rarely designed to quickly study links "between diagnoses and specific vaccination events."

The letter did not specifically discuss anti-vaccine activism.

While in Samoa, Kennedy met with anti-vaccine activists, including one who helped arrange the trip with a U.S. Embassy employee, the AP and the Guardian previously reported.

Months later, with vaccination rates still dangerously low, measles broke out, sickening thousands.

Public health experts have said their efforts to address the outbreak were hampered by anti-vaccine activists, some of whom they claim were emboldened by Kennedy's visit.

Spokespeople for CHD and HHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.

Wyden is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, which has oversight into Kennedy's health department, when Democrats retake Congress in January. Alsobrooks serves on the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which also oversees the department.

The same senators on Wednesday announced a separate investigation into hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of gifts reportedly given last year to Kennedy by a donor and former employee.
