#5723. QuantumScape Has An Osprey Up Its Solid-State EV Battery Sleeve

Federal policy makers orchestrated an EV sales crash in the US last year, only to see electrification stakeholders gradually piece together a comeback focusing on cars that hit the affordability MSRP of $30,000 or less. New, higher-performing solid-state EV batteries are also inching their way towards the market, with the US startup QuantumScape among the innovators contributing some fresh news in recent weeks (for the record, Finland’s Donut Labs is another).

As the name indicates, a solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte of a conventional lithium-ion battery with a solid material. If that sounds like a deep electrochemical challenge, its is. Nevertheless, science loves a challenge, and so do electrification stakeholders who are determined to sharpen the contrast between EVs and gasmobiles. Compared to the current generation of EV batteries, solid-state technology meets a higher bar for energy density and other performance benchmarks, while avoiding the use of volatile chemicals (see more solid-state background here)

High tech ceramics have emerged as one of the options, and that is where QuantumScape has set its sights. The company launched in 2010 and it surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in 2012, when Volkswagen dropped word of its interest in the solid-state forumula.

QS has been focusing its attention on developing a lithium-metal formula for the anode (the part of a battery that collects a charge), by tweaking the separator, which is the part of a battery that serves as a buffer on the electrolyte.

“A solid-state lithium-metal battery…replaces the polymer separator used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid-state separator. The replacement of the separator enables the carbon or silicon anode used in conventional lithium-ion batteries to be replaced with a lithium-metal anode,” QS explains.

To ice the solid-state cake, the QS anode does not make an appearance during the battery manufacturing process. It self-forms as part of the battery’s first charging cycle.

QS has accumulated a string of investors and affiliations since 2012, capped by a hookup with the legacy firm Corning last year aimed at developing a manufacturing system that accommodates its ceramic separator.

The latest news takes QS farther into all-solid state technology, this time with a focus on the cathode, under the trade name Osprey.

“Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell,” the company explained in a press statement on November 11.

“Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries,” the company elaborates. The QS blog further explains that Osprey is a “solid-state platform that allows developers of sulfide-based solid-state batteries to incorporate QS technology into their all-solid-state battery (ASSB) development programs.”

Don’t get too excited just yet — the cathode work is still in the early stages of validation — but QS is now confident that its data will stand up under public scrutiny. In addition to safety improvements compared to conventional Li-ion batteries, QS checks a list of additional performance boxes for ASSBs:

“Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions

Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes

Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure

Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F)

Want more details? Check out the QS blog, where the company takes a deeper dive into the new cathode.

As for why QS is working the sulfide angle, that’s a good question. “Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications,” QS notes. Despite those challenges, QS also notes the sulfide formula continues to attract widespread interest in the solid-state field, due to its high level of conductivity and ease of processing. If all goes according to plan, the Osprey platform will enable solid-state battery developers to continue pursuing sulfide to their hearts’ content.

“The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits,” explains QS president and CEO Dr. Siva Sivaram, “As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations.”

As another indication that sulfide stakeholders are not out chasing rainbows, take a look at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, part of a sprawling network of research facilities under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy. ORNL has just published a new study in the journal Energy Materials under the title, “Operando neutron radiography reveals calendar aging-induced lithium redistribution and back-diffusion in thick-cathode all-solid-state batteries.”

As the title indicates, the researchers deployed a neutron radiation tool to probe the inner workings of lithium batteries while they are in operation, enabling them to deliver a precise map of the degradation process that has bedeviled the sulfide field. They also delivered a roadmap for further work:

“Based on these findings from calendar aging, we envision future formation strategies should be redesigned to minimize sustained potential gradients while stabilizing interphases, for example through optimized composite electronic percolation and catholyte or coating materials and validated with time-resolved neutron imaging to establish transport-informed, durability-first conditioning rules that generalize across cathode loadings and operating temperatures.”

Got all that? The real question is why a federal research institution is still delivering advanced analyses leading to the next generation of EV batteries that outperform conventional batteries while improving EV safety and reducing overall costs. After all, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have expended considerable time and effort to stop, if not reverse, EV sales in the US. In addition to prematurely killing off the $7,500 EV tax credit last fall, the President also tried (and ultimately failed) to claw back funds from the federal NEVI public EV charging station program.

Readers, take a guess at the answer in the discussion thread. One possible explanation is the energy storage angle. While the President’s whackadoodle “American Energy Dominance Policy” dials down solar and wind (especially wind), it supports practically every other domestic energy resource including nuclear, biomass, geothermal, and hydropower alongside fossil fuels, with energy storage also making a substantial appearance.

The electronic war of the future is another factor to consider, with crewless vehicles and “anti-idling” kits serving as a sort of gateway drug that demonstrates the logistical and tactical advantages of battery power, silent running, and a lower heat signature compared to diesel fuel.

#5722. At $2,600, Is This 1999 Ford Expedition XLT Worth The Trek?

In today's used car market, it's hard to find a vehicle that offers more bang (or space) for your buck than Ford's Expedition. Today's Nice Price or No Dice '99 XLT might be a prime example, but, as always, you'll get the final word on that.

Daimler-Benz deserves kudos for being one of the few stalwart automakers to still sell a traditional estate model here in the U.S. Mercedes has offered a wagon on the E-Class platform for nearly half a century, beginning with the W123 in 1977. Yesterday, we looked at that model's prodigy of nearly two decades later (and with only one major model change): a 1995 Mercedes-Benz E320 Estate.

That car came to us in stately silver, with the promise of proper maintenance and no mechanical issues. It also had all the wagon-y goodness one could want, with a spacious load area and a fold-up rear-facing third row to take us all back to our formative years. That was all enough to make the classic Benz a solid contender at its $10,250 asking price. We all circled our wagons and awarded the longroof a razor-thin 51% 'Nice Price' win.

Yesterday's Mercedes held a lot of appeal, with its classic proportions, legendary build quality, and status-symbol three-pointed star hood ornament. What if, however, you needed something similar, but with vastly more room inside, more pedestrian mechanicals to make maintenance easier, and a price tag that eschewed any sense of status-seeking? If those criteria fit your expectations and budget (more on that in a minute), then the 1999 Ford Expedition XLT 4X4 we have under adjudication today should fit the bill.

Ford introduced the Expedition for the 1997 model year, basing it on the then-new F-Series pickup chassis and styling it to look like the company's wildly popular, and more fun-sized Explorer. Nominally, the Expedition replaced the long-in-the-tooth two-door Bronco in Ford's sales-leading truck lineup. Sorry, O.J. It also finally gave Ford a direct competitor to Chevrolet's long-running Suburban three-row SUV, something the company had never offered before.

The mad mix of solid F-Series stoutness and Explorer-curious-buyer-friendly style proved a winning combination for the Expedition, and even more so for the Lincoln Navigator that it spawned, the model that arguably has kept the lights on at Ford's fancy-pants brand for more than three decades.

This Expedition comes in appliance white over an institutional but dutifully long-wearing gray mousefur-and-plastic interior. There's nothing particularly fancy or luxurious about this large SUV, which is laudable for anyone seeking basic but dang-big transportation. And dang-big it is.

If you were buying Fords at Costco, this would be the model the box stores would offer, and you'd probably have to buy two of them, connected by a plastic grab handle. The deets are: a 119-inch wheelbase, supporting over 200 inches of overall length. With over six and a half feet of overall width, the truck offers more than 63 inches of interior shoulder room for stretching out or for road trip games of slug bug.

This Expedition is claimed to have a V8, but the ad doesn't specify which V8 is under its hood. Standard equipment was Ford's 4.6-liter SOHC Triton V8 offering 215 horsepower and 290 pound-feet of torque. As an option, buyers could opt for a 5.4-liter displacement edition making 230 horses and raising torque output to 325 pound-feet.

Whether or not the engine makes a difference at this Expedition's price (more on that in a minute) will have to be seen. What we do know is that behind the engine is a standard four-speed automatic transmission and, as this is a 4X4 edition, a two-speed Borg-Warner transfer case feeding Ford's ControlTrac pushbutton 4WD.

According to the ad, that drivetrain has confidently pushed the truck to 143,279 miles, and it seems ready for even more, as the seller claims the truck is mechanically sound and has no warning lights nagging from the instrument cluster. The exterior is free of dents or significant paint failure, and it rolls on factory alloys fitted with tires with plenty of life left. The cabin looks just as serviceable as it is unexciting, with only a cracked, worn console armrest as an obvious sign of age and use. This truck has all the basics covered, too, with front and rear climate control, cruise, power windows and locks, and what looks like a towing package. A clean title and get-out-of-jail-free card from the smog tester are additional check marks in this Expedition's favor.

Okay, so that's all well and good, but what would something this size and with these capabilities rightfully cost? This Expedition—which appears to do it all—asks $2,600. See? I told you we would get to that value proposition. This isn't an outlier, either: everywhere you look, prices on old Expeditions are down in the bottom of the well with poor, unfortunate Timmy.

For all of us who have lamented that the entry point for the used car market has (like everything) risen substantially since the pandemic, here is a class of vehicles that the valuation tsunami passed by unaffected. It's like discovering a valley of big, dopey dinosaurs right in your own backyard. Two reasons these Fords are likely so cheap are that they get really bad fuel economy, averaging around 15 mpg no matter what, and that, regardless of displacement, the Triton V8s fitted to these models have a reputation for spitting out spark plugs like expectorated loogies. Both issues are expensive considerations in themselves.

Regardless, we now need you to choose whether this Expedition is worth even that $2,600 asking, or if it's best to pass on the big—but cheap—beast.

Planning a family road trip usually starts with excitement. Everyone gets involved in choosing the destination, checking the route, preparing snacks, and packing luggage for the journey. Parents make sure the kids have entertainment, while other family members prepare drinks, travel essentials, and everything needed for a comfortable ride. However, amid all the preparation, some easily overlooked vehicle interior problems can turn into unexpected inconveniences along the way. A little mud brought into the cabin, difficulty climbing into a tall pickup, or small belongings scattered across the seats may not seem like serious issues before departure. Yet after several hours on the road, these minor problems can become frustrating, particularly when traveling with children or older family members. A comfortable road trip is not only about reaching the destination; it is also about making sure everyone can enjoy the journey without constantly dealing with unnecessary mess and discomfort.

Family travel puts a vehicle’s interior to the test. One of the most common challenges is keeping the floor clean. Children may step into the vehicle with muddy shoes after outdoor activities, while food crumbs, spilled drinks, and snack wrappers can quickly make the factory carpet look messy. Cleaning these stains can take time, especially after a long trip. Another issue is getting in and out of taller SUVs and pickup trucks. Although their higher ground clearance is useful for different driving conditions, the height can make entry and exit less convenient for young children and older passengers. Repeatedly climbing into the cabin may require extra effort and assistance. Finally, there is the problem of small items getting everywhere. Toys, charging cables, tissues, water bottles, and travel accessories often end up under seats or scattered around the cabin. When passengers cannot find what they need, the journey can become less organized. These problems may be ordinary, but addressing them before departure can make a noticeable difference to the overall travel experience.

These accessories do not change a vehicle’s engine performance, horsepower, or driving capability. Their value lies in improving the everyday experience of using the vehicle, particularly when several passengers and plenty of belongings are involved. Floor mats help reduce the amount of dirt and moisture reaching the original carpet, making post-trip cleanup less demanding. Running boards offer a more convenient stepping point for passengers, which can be especially helpful for children and older family members when entering or leaving a taller vehicle. Meanwhile, storage boxes help prevent small belongings from taking over the cabin, allowing passengers to find their essentials more easily. #5720. Managing Metastases in Advanced Prostate Cancer

— Beyond Diagnosis continues with Christopher Wee on radiation therapy and multidisciplinary care

Developed in partnership with the Our Partner

In "Beyond Diagnosis: Metastatic Castration-Sensitive Prostate Cancer," Cleveland Clinic oncologist Christopher Wee, MD, and host John Mangels discuss how clinicians can guide patients through the growing complexities of treatment for metastatic disease.

Each installment of this series explores key moments in patient care, including building trust, navigating evolving therapies, aligning treatment goals, and supporting shared decision-making.

In this fourth episode, Wee discusses the role of radiation in managing metastatic disease, strategies for treating bone metastases and preventing skeletal complications, and the importance of multidisciplinary care in balancing disease control with quality of life.

The following is a transcript of their remarks:

Mangels: Welcome to "Beyond Diagnosis," where we talk with doctors about treatment decisions and communicating with patients. I'm your host, John Mangels.

Treatment of metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer has changed significantly in the last decade. Those changes are creating new opportunities and new complexities for both physicians and patients. How do clinicians choose among expanded treatment options? How do they navigate decisions involving efficacy and risk, quality of life, and patient preferences?

We'll explore those issues and more with our guest, Dr. Christopher Wee. Dr. Wee is a physician in Cleveland Clinic's genitourinary medical oncology program. A large part of his practice involves patients with prostate cancer. Dr. Wee, thanks so much for joining us today.

Mangels: Metastatic disease involves more complexities and more complications potentially than localized prostate cancer. Is your approach to treat metastases individually? Do you try and control them systemically? What's your approach on that?

Wee: Historically, metastatic disease has been a systemic therapy situation, because the spots that you can see on imaging likely underrepresent the true burden of disease. There could be micrometastases elsewhere. And so that's why we don't go and necessarily go after each individual metastasis.

However, there's a caveat, and this is an evolving science. Radiation is becoming an integral part in certain situations. So if someone were to have low-volume de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, there is a survival benefit per the STAMPEDE trial to do prostate-directed radiotherapy. Sometimes we'll even consider metastasis-directed therapy in those situations. And then if something were to become oligoprogressive to castrate-resistant, so let's say someone has castration-sensitive prostate cancer, metastatic, and the PSA [prostate-specific antigen] starts rising, but there's only one or two spots that are really lighting up on a repeat PET, there are emerging data suggesting that radiation or often SBRT [stereotactic body radiotherapy] can be a benefit to that patient because then if they can get control, they don't have to necessarily switch treatment.

So this is evolving science. I think this is where it's very important to have a multidisciplinary team evaluate these situations, but systemic therapy is still the backbone of treatment of metastatic disease.

Mangels: We've talked a lot already about patient communication. When patients learn that their prostate cancer has spread to their bones or say an organ like the liver, that's bound to be frightening to them. How do you help them understand what those findings mean without completely eradicating hope?

Wee: I think it's frightening because of the uncertainty, and I wish I could sometimes give more certainty to patients like this. Most patients want an honest answer. They don't want sugarcoating. So I'll ask a patient, "Do you mind if I'm upfront with you?" Vast majority of the time they want to know. This is generally considered, in historically speaking, not a curable situation, but some patients can live for years, many years. I don't know at this point. Our goal is to try to give you the best outcome possible, and we do this with these treatments and we go from there.

If patients start asking more specifically about life expectancies, again, at the time of metastatic diagnosis, the median overall survival is years. So it's really hard to predict at that point what this is going to look like.

Mangels: And that's so important to emphasize that incurable doesn't mean untreatable.

Mangels: And then I'm guessing the discussion about patient treatment goals, quality of life, all the things we've talked about before becomes even more important.

So bones are by far the most common site of metastasis in prostate cancer. Beyond controlling the cancer itself, what are your priorities when you're treating a patient with skeletal metastases? Are you looking at managing pain? Are you looking at trying to prevent fractures?

Wee: So in castration-sensitive disease, the primary treatment is actually just using systemic therapy, ADT [androgen deprivation therapy] plus ARPI [androgen receptor pathway inhibitor], plus/minus chemo. The role of a bone-modifying agent such as a bisphosphonate like zoledronic acid [Reclast] or RANKL ligand like denosumab [Prolia] is reserved primarily for patients who have osteoporosis. So a bone scan would be helpful, bone density scan. And if someone has osteoporosis, that should be treated appropriately.

If a patient progresses to castration-resistant disease, there is an indication to give a bone-modifying agent to prevent a skeletal-related metastasis. So that's where the conversation comes into even if a patient doesn't have osteoporosis, if they have osseous metastases, there should be consideration to be giving a bone-modifying agent in castration-resistant disease. If there's a symptomatic spot that's causing a lot of trouble, that's a great time to also consider palliative radiation.

Mangels: Let's talk about radiation. When do you bring in radiation oncology and is the goal of the radiation to treat the tumor or to treat the pain or something else?

Wee: In metastatic prostate cancer, there's generally a few reasons. One, as we discussed previously, in de novo low-volume metastatic disease, primary prostatic radiation should be considered due to an overall survival benefit in STAMPEDE trial, but then also palliative radiation to specific spots if they're painful and metastasis-directed therapy.

So this is where the gray area comes in. So let's say someone has low-volume metastatic disease, just a couple of bone spots per se -- and we're getting this more often now that we have PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen] PET -- or a couple lymph nodes only. We had talked about previously how the standard of care metastatic disease is indefinite ADT, but what if you were able to zap all the spots of disease with radiation? Could you give a defined course of treatment to give a treatment-free interval? It's unclear the optimal duration and everything, but it's something we talk about with patients.

And anecdotally, some of these patients can get prolonged disease-free intervals where they don't have to be on treatment necessarily. And so that's something where it's shared decision-making with the patient.

Mangels: Are there particular patterns of metastatic spread or symptomatology or lab results, clinical findings that make you think, "Wow, I really need to think about whether this approach with this patient needs to change or not"?

Wee: I think there are two reasons why we would want to change. If one, the treatment regimen we're not doing is not working, or two, if it is not having manageable toxicity. Those are two reasons to change treatment.

Sometimes, this is not the most common situation, but sometimes despite the PSA being low, a patient could be clinically doing worse. They may be having more fatigue, more weight loss. That should be a red flag. At that time, usually I would re-image with conventional imaging if the PSA is low, because what you worry about in those situations is could this be differentiating into another process such as a neuroendocrine differentiation of prostate cancer or small cell neuroendocrine? And that's a lot more aggressive, at which point it needs to be managed differently with a lot more aggressive therapy sometimes.

Mangels: We talked a couple of seconds ago about bringing radiation oncology in, but that sort of opens the door to the importance of multidisciplinary care in these patients. Let's talk about that. You've got orthopedic oncology, I'm guessing, pain management, palliative care, rehab. Talk about how you coordinate all of those and involve all those and why they're important to be involved.

Wee: Absolutely. So radiation oncology is probably the most common one we work with, obviously. Palliative medicine with the symptom support, especially if there's pain involved because we can really improve patients' quality of life and oftentimes extend survival if we have good palliative care.

We're increasingly using our colleagues in nuclear medicine, both from a diagnostic standpoint with the PSMA PET scans as well as therapeutics with radioligand therapy. So this is one of the exciting parts of being a medical oncologist is the team-sport nature of this and how we can all work together to try to do what's best for the patient.

Mangels: Thanks so much for your insights, Dr. Wee. And thank you for joining us on Beyond Diagnosis, where we explore not just what physicians know, but how to effectively and compassionately share that knowledge with patients. See you next time.

#5719. 2027 Acura Integra Type S Gets A Type R-Inspired Heritage Edition

The Acura Integra Type S is, unquestionably, one of my favorite cars on the market right now, if not my outright favorite car on the market, full stop. It's gorgeous, it's fun, it's just about everything you could want in a sport sedan. There's one thing the Integra Type S has always lacked, though, something that Acura has only now finally seen fit to give: Yellow paint. This is the Integra Type S Heritage Edition, and it comes in the only color that matters.

For 2027, Acura is giving the Integra Type S with a few updates. Most of them are interior changes, new trim pieces and upholstery options, and convenience features like position-memorizing seats, but the big change is the introduction of the new limited-run model to the lineup. The U.S. is getting just 700 Heritage Edition cars, all of them decked out in a color the company is calling Blazing Phoenix Yellow. It's not the same paint code as the old Type R of yore, but Acura says it's a brighter and more saturated replacement.

The Heritage Edition is just a cosmetic package, there's no power upgrades or trick suspension here, but it does go deeper than just the yellow paint. The car also gets blacked-out badges, a titanium shift knob, and copper wheels — all from Acura's existing accessory catalog, but bundled together for this model. Each car is also done up with a black interior, which includes yellow accent stitching that matches the Heritage Edition's exterior. (That yellow stitching is found on any 2027 Integra Type S with the black interior, not just this special edition.)

The rest of the Integra Type S' changes for 2027 aren't huge — gloss black mirror caps and wheels, yellow brake calipers, and a mirror that automatically tilts down when you back up aren't exactly game-changing upgrades — but there's not much that can be done to improve on the Integra's existing state. Blazing Phoenix Yellow is enough, and I truly hope that these cars aren't all snatched up by investors to be squirreled away in climate-controlled garages. Let these things drive, let them breathe like the DC2 Integras by which they're inspired. I want to see these out on the roads.

#5717. Four of Seven Dutch Green Hydrogen Projects Have Been Cancelled. The Subsidies Keep Coming.

The Netherlands awarded €783.5 million in subsidies to seven green hydrogen projects in 2022. Together they were supposed to deliver 1,150 MW of electrolysis capacity. Four years later, four projects representing 550 MW have been cancelled, and none of the original seven is operating. The November 2 parliamentary answers also confirm that the government cannot say when electrolytic hydrogen will become commercially viable without dedicated subsidies. Another €780 million is reserved for a future subsidy round anyway.

The TFIE Strategy Briefing follows what happened to the Dutch projects, what the government’s own cost and demand revisions imply, and which industrial activities could prosper without the hydrogen market originally forecast.

The €783.5 million was awarded, not spent. Roughly €150 million had been disbursed under the programme when the parliamentary answers were published. That distinction matters, especially when assessing potential losses to taxpayers. It does not make the project record look good. The Dutch state has spent four years supporting a group of plants that has so far delivered no operating capacity, while almost half the planned megawatts have been withdrawn.

The price assumptions were difficult to defend from the start. Officials say the original subsidy decisions reflected expectations that renewable hydrogen would cost around €2/kg by 2030 and become competitive with fossil-derived hydrogen within a decade. Making a kilogram by electrolysis typically requires about 50–55 kWh of electricity. Even at €50/MWh, a very cheap assumption for dependable electricity supplied to a European industrial facility, that power costs €2.50–€2.75 per kilogram before capital recovery, maintenance, water treatment, compression or delivery. Buying electricity only during the cheapest hours lowers the energy bill but leaves the electrolyser idle for longer, increasing the capital cost per kilogram produced. Eurostat’s latest industrial electricity data show how low the €50/MWh assumption is relative to ordinary non-household electricity prices, although large electrolysers would negotiate different contracts.

There are established industrial uses for hydrogen, particularly in chemicals and refining. The Dutch policy went considerably further, assuming domestic electrolysis could grow into a competitive source of energy for processes where direct electricity would often be cheaper. The cancellations have arrived alongside retreat from those anticipated markets, not as an isolated string of engineering setbacks. Lower-than-expected demand and expensive production are undermining the case for both the plants and the infrastructure intended to connect them.

The government’s September energy planning already gives hydrogen much less work in building heat and electricity generation. It also projects substantially less industrial hydrogen demand than earlier plans. Nevertheless, the proposed response includes more production subsidies, obligations for some industrial customers to buy renewable hydrogen, and measures to support a national pipeline network. Those choices keep public policy committed to volumes that commercial buyers have not shown they can afford.

The network has its own deteriorating economics. The Netherlands Court of Audit found that estimated investment had risen from €1.5 billion to €3.8 billion. Gasunie/Hynetwork Services estimated startup losses of up to €2.5 billion against a €750 million grant. These are forecasts, not bills already paid. But a pipeline system designed for a large future hydrogen market becomes harder to finance when that market contracts. Higher tariffs would make hydrogen less attractive to the customers it needs. Additional subsidies shift the burden elsewhere. The Court of Audit laid out the problem in December 2025.

Dutch chemical manufacturing, steel processing and port industries do not need to disappear as hydrogen expectations shrink. Some energy-intensive feedstocks can be produced where clean electricity is cheaper and imported for further manufacturing in the Netherlands. Industrial heat pumps and direct electric processes avoid producing and transporting hydrogen in the first place. Smaller refineries will also need less hydrogen as petroleum demand declines. These changes have different consequences for particular companies and workers, but they offer a more credible starting point for an industrial strategy than a hydrogen-volume target.

The government now faces another subsidy round with evidence it did not have in 2022: cancelled projects, higher costs, much smaller demand expectations and a pipeline investment whose customers are uncertain. It should evaluate the industrial products being made, the cost of the available decarbonization routes and the amount of hydrogen that those routes actually require before funding another large tranche of production capacity. Otherwise the next awards risk preserving yesterday’s forecasts at tomorrow’s expense.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis examines the project record, subsidy assumptions, pipeline exposure and alternatives for Dutch industrial production. It includes the implications for ammonia, steel and refining that are beyond the scope of this CleanTechnica article.

#5716. What Happens in Vegas Should Inform the Rest of the Country

This research brief highlights lessons from Nevada’s workplace heat standard.

Coauthored with Barrak Alahmad and Yazan Alwadi, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Most U.S. states lack formal workplace standards for dangerous heat. This long-standing gap puts millions of working people at risk every year, especially as climate change increases the intensity and duration of hot seasons across the country.

Many lawmakers and worker protection agencies are now trying to fill the gap, in part by learning from existing standards in California, Colorado, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington State.

However, not all existing heat standards are created equal. Nevada’s workplace heat standard in particular lacks several evidence-based elements that are common to other states, including temperature thresholds that trigger specific safeguards. Instead, Nevada allows employers to decide at what point to provide heat protections to their workers—a choice that many industry representatives want replicated elsewhere.

This research brief uses heat complaints lodged by Nevada workers to make the case that there are, in fact, clear data-driven temperature thresholds that can be implemented across industries. These thresholds should be an essential part of any system of heat protections that includes water, rest, shade, acclimatization, and other safeguards on the job.

What Happens in Vegas Should Inform the Rest of the Country: Lessons Learned from Nevada’s Heat Complaints Database (PDF)

Article from NRDC. By Juanita Constible, Senior Advocate, Environmental Health.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Elon Musk wants to merge his biggest companies, giving Robinhood addicts a single ticker to watch to satisfy their obsession with Musk's weird antics. Tesla and SpaceX are still figuring out how to make a deal, despite the midterm blue wave which could meaningfully impede the merger. From Reuters:

Nov 12 (Reuters) – SpaceX and Tesla are progressing in their merger negotiations, and a ​deal could be announced as early as ‌December, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The proposed merger would unify Elon Musk's ​AI, robotics, EV and aerospace ambitions under ​a single corporate roof, though it faces steep ⁠regulatory hurdles over SpaceX's US defense contracts ​and Tesla's reliance on China.

Mercedes-Benz, noted German automaker, has decided that being German is just too expensive. The company's latest round of negotiations with unions hasn't yielded any cost savings, so the company is now halting new spending on its German factories — and considering closing some altogether. From Automotive News:

FRANKFURT — Mercedes-Benz is freezing investment in its German plants and exploring site closures after failing to agree with worker representatives on labor cost cuts.

The automaker made the move after talks with its works council and union stalled, according to an interview with executive board members shared on the company's intranet.

Mercedes' production chief Michael Schiebe said in the interview that management had "jointly decided to halt all further investments in our German locations."

Mercedes' reasoning is that labor in Germany is more expensive than in Eastern Europe or the United States, which is the sort of reasoning an employer would use to evade such considerations like cost of living changes. I imagine the union members involved will have something to say about losing their jobs entirely.

One automaker, though, is actually climbing the rankings: Rivian. From Automotive News:

Auto industry newcomers Tesla and Rivian are taking over the U.S. electric vehicle market following last year's repeal of the federal tax credit, as traditional brands turn to gas models and hybrids, analysts said.

While EV registrations fell 44 percent in September compared with the record set a year earlier, Tesla registrations slipped a relatively modest 27 percent and Rivian posted a gain, the most recent data from Mobility Global showed. The data does not include hybrids.

Rivian's share of the EV market in September rose to 7.6 percent, a gain of 4.5 percentage points. Combined, the two brands captured nearly two-thirds of all EV registrations for the month.

INDIANAPOLIS — Today, Hoosiers turned out to speak against toxic coal ash pollution at the EPA’s public hearing on Indiana’s proposed Coal Ash permitting program, which would allow the state to disregard federal protections for communities in favor of statewide rules that would provide fewer safeguards.

The EPA is also proposing to approve the Indiana Department of Environmental Management’s (IDEM) application without considering IDEM’s track record of allowing dangerous coal ash contamination.

Indiana is home to more coal ash dumps than any other state. Over 100 coal ash landfills and ponds at more than 20 plant sites contain approximately 134 million cubic yards of toxic coal ash — the equivalent to a football field piled nearly 12 miles high with coal ash, twice as high as Mount Everest.

Nicole Chandler, Southwest Indiana Beyond Coal Organizer: “My home, Evansville, Indiana, lies right along the Ohio River — one of the most polluted rivers in the country. With Evansville being in the heart of Indiana coal country, we’ve become an environmental sacrifice zone: negative health outcomes from polluted air, water, and soil all harm my community. Indiana’s coal ash regulations are even less stringent than federal rules. If the EPA approves IDEM’s proposal, there could be coal ash dumps that continue leaking indefinitely if IDEM doesn’t act fast enough. We need the EPA to make sure coal ash rules protect our communities, not make it easier for coal plants to pollute.”

Megan Anderson, Senior Campaign Coordinator, Beyond Coal: “Hundreds of Hoosiers near coal ash dumps are on well water, making getting regulations right a matter of life and death. The EPA is derelicting its duties if the agency approves of Indiana’s inadequate coal ash program that leaves Hoosiers and our environment vulnerable to further coal ash contamination.”

#5712. IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry

SPECIAL BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

QDC26 shows progress in the hardware, software and tooling around quantum computing as customers look for evidence of better outcomes.

IBM Corp.’s Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week marked a change in emphasis. IBM claims that researchers have demonstrated quantum advantage in 2026 by working with the classical computing community. Its public presentations showed progress in processors, error correction, scientific software and the integration of quantum with conventional computing.

The company’s quantum leader, Jay Gambetta (pictured), also set a new target. The next big milestone comes by demonstrating industry impact by 2028, conditional on collaboration across enterprise application researchers and the classical and quantum communities.

Our key takeaway is that IBM is assembling more of the full system required to turn a quantum experiment into useful scientific work. Hardware is important, but the real innovation will come from software. Importantly, the tools that help a scientist formulate a problem, run it across different computing resources, check the result and understand the economics are where much of the innovation is headed. These capabilities address several of the barriers customers described to us in our spring quantum tour of major scientific research labs; and the issues discussed with technologists on our Quantum 101 Series at theCUBE’s NYSE studio.

Despite the progress being made, the remaining gaps and challenges are many. Quantum science is advancing but impact on industries is still years away. Better software is the key to making dramatic improvements in quantum performance and a new service capability can attract researchers. But if a chemist needs to understand the deep nuances of quantum computing, it limits adoption. We believe the next phase of innovation will focus on abstracting quantum complexities and making measurable improvements in simplicity to drive further usage.

In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine IBM’s public QDC proclamations through the prism of our spring interviews with six quantum and supercomputing experts. We add customer perspectives from our partner Qualitate, assess the implications of IBM’s foundry investments and consider what evidence would signal that progress is moving from scientific advantage to industry impact.

IBM’s progress comes into better focus when evaluating its milestones separately. IBM’s goal of demonstrating Quantum Advantage by 2026 is generally accepted as met, based on achieving particular computation superiority relative to today’s classical methods. But to truly show industry impact, IBM needs to show results make a difference to an organization. Milestones around fault-tolerant architectures will increasingly focus on the ability to sustain reliable computation in the face of errors. Progress in one category will definitely support another but it’s useful to look at milestones and proof points separately as shown below.

IBM deserves high marks for achieving that advantage but is subject to scrutiny. Gambetta’s keynote described classical researchers overtaking quantum results, claims being withdrawn as classical makes improvements, and subsequent quantum work moving the needle in favor of quantum again. This of course is how a competitive scientific ecosystem should operate. We’re eager to see the leapfrogging end and await a day where a quantum advantage becomes sustainable with clear evidence that classical computing has no chance of catching up for specified use cases.

Observers can rightly be concerned that incorrect inferences may be drawn from the term “advantage.” The phrase can sound like a statement of superiority. But if that advantage is not consistently held, then the broader industry might remain skeptical. The same applies to verifying that a customer outcome is attributable an underlying scientific model powered by quantum.

A public Allstate example is useful and illustrates the difference. IBM described underwriting-optimization results as comparable to classical optimization schemes. That can represent progress, but it does not show that quantum has delivered a superior underwriting outcome. Customers need to decide how much they are prepared to invest in learning before a measurable benefit appears. IBM, in our view, is working hard to simplify the heavy lift and broaden adoption.

The researchers we interviewed in spring 2026 for World Quantum Day were already thinking beyond the hardware. Their concerns included application selection, reliability, integration, software complexity and the ability to preserve optionality as hardware evolves. These were six independent editorial interviews conducted on theCUBE, made possible by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., across five institutions, offering a view of the work required to make quantum useful. The discussions were hosted by this author and Paul Gillin, managing editor at SiliconANGLE.

The following table highlights the to priority stated by each researcher at the time and our take on how IBM has responded in the past 6-9 months.

IBM is directing effort toward problems that these practitioners identified months earlier. We believe that is a strong indicator of product relevance, an even more important than hardware milestones.

It also gives us a more reasonable test of true progress. A scientist must be able to attack a meaningful problem with less setup effort, run it more reliably and compare the result with a credible classical alternative. IBM’s public announcements show capabilities intended to support that progression and the gaps identified this spring by our researcher friends. Thus far, however, they don’t show how broadly researchers can complete their tasks without specialist assistance. IBM shared additional capabilities to a small group of industry analysts under NDA, which look encouraging.

Some of the most interesting material in Chicago concerned ordinary operational friction. In the public developer sessions, IBM described experiments interrupted by sleeping laptops, dead notebook sessions, running out of memory or tokens, and lost work in process. In quantum research, as with AI YOLO training runs, they add expense and blockers to work that already requires specialized expertise.

Managed workflows address this through simplification by moving execution into a hosted environment with conventional computing resources and tools to capture and save work in process. Researchers can associate quantum jobs with the workflow and monitor consumption across both quantum and classical support infrastructure. That creates a basis for repeating experiments and understanding where resources are consumed and how to optimize the complete process.

Take the chemistry approaches discussed at the event. Researchers can divide a larger molecular problem into smaller parts, use quantum or classical computing methods for appropriate parts and combine the results. At QDC26, IBM described improvements in classical algorithms that support the processing of quantum jobs. Classical solving steps can become a major bottlenecks and represent opportunities for optimization.

The relevant focus is increasingly the complete research workflow. Here we’re referring to the preparation, the quantum work, the classical processing and the validation. This expands the opportunity for IBM and its partners because more of the work can be supported through its software and services. It also shines a light on how the economic case needs to evolve, with a focus on the cost of an outcome.

Faster quantum hardware alone is not the answer. Conversely, better classical software can make quantum experiments much more productive. Both are developments that came into focus at QDC26. Customers need enough visibility to identify the bottlenecks and implement improvements.

IBM’s pronouncements about AI are expected to address barriers raised in our spring interviews – the complexity of translating domain knowledge into a working quantum experiment. IBM must provide skills that assist with choosing methods, workflows, applying classical algorithms and the like. And validating implementations before longer, more expensive runs take place. Our developer conversations at the event underscore demand for AI assistance with calls for simpler packaging and managed services.

We believe this marks is an important near-term relationship between AI and quantum. AI can help scientists use quantum computing more effectively before quantum delivers a broadly demonstrated improvement in AI itself. The immediate opportunity is to simplify – reducing the effort required to apply specialized software and infrastructure.

This requirement has implications for how scientific software is packaged. A library contains reusable code. Increasingly, skills will supply context and guidelines for selecting and applying that code. As skills improve, we expect more of the integration work to be assisted by software. The value of a mature library will still depend on its performance and suitability for the task at hand. The public QDC releases include libraries, mapping tools and AI skills together; they hint toward an evolution in how software will be used in the future.

Another gap is accountability. For example, what happens if a workflow executes but uses invalid scientific assumptions. An AI-generated configuration can appear valid while making a poor trade-off between accuracy and cost, for example. In our view, a useful abstraction must maintain the ability to understand those AI decisions and validate them in terms that a domain expert/scientist comprehends.

This is where customer evidence must become more specific in our view. For example, can a chemist repeat useful work without a vendor team guiding them every step? Can another scientist reproduce the result? Can the organization see what exactly changed between runs? We would place considerable weight on those conditions when judging whether easier programming translates into broader scientific adoption.

Chemistry and materials are fields that provide a strong connection between our spring interviews and the public QDC discussions. Johansson at CSC emphasized the challenge of modeling interacting electrons. Beck at Oak Ridge described materials and chemistry research with potential relevance to fusion and biology. IBM’s sessions discussed tools for decomposing problems and processing results across quantum and conventional systems working in tandem.

We view these fields as particularly credible places to look for early useful applications because the scientific problems involve quantum behavior. That is a reason to prioritize research that benefits from quantum. Problem scope, accuracy and economics (or feasibility) relative to conventional methods will determine the ultimate usefulness of quantum.

IBM’s performance progress is notable, but its points of comparison are instructive. Its headline 25-fold improvement in maximum circuit throughput compares Nighthawk r2 with Heron. Several application improvements also compare newer IBM quantum systems with earlier ones. Those figures demonstrate progress within IBM’s generations but a customer still needs a comparison with the best practical classical approach to the same problem.

The mot useful metric in our view is the cost and time required to obtain a validated outcome. The calculation should include all aspects of conventional preprocessing and post-processing, the quantum work done, job completion times and the intensity of the technical skills required perform and validate the result. Importantly, an important future measure is whether the process can be consistently repeated at scale.

Customers should absolutely invest before quantum consistently wins. The key is to identify those investments as a learning experience.

Post-quantum cryptography or PQC is a topic we unpacked at theCUBE’s Quantum Readiness Day this past September. Qualitate customer survey findings add another dimension to our PQC analysis. But don’t confuse PQC spend with quantum application adoption.

A query of Qualitate’s interview data on quantum adoption focuses heavily on PQC, a tactical topic that is top of mind for enterprises today. Organizations are spending to prepare existing information systems to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. The data include customers already taking action, as well as those evaluating.

“Now is the time we’re really starting to go all in on post quantum cryptography.”

The same participant, a technology lead at a professional services company, explains the rationale in terms of future loss avoidance:

“We anticipate that this will significantly save us on dealing with enormous crises in the future.”

Today’s enterprise focus as it relates to quantum is on modernizing cryptography. This is far ahead of investing to find useful applications for a quantum computer. Today’s practitioners are consumed with deploying and securing agents and making AI trustworthy. Quantum applications, other than PQC, are not top-of-mind for most enterprise customers. Security work to protect conventional systems is tactical and there’s little evidence of interest in running workloads on quantum hardware within organizations today.

NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024 and encourages organizations to begin transitioning. Its guidance also explains the risk that adversaries collect encrypted information today for possible decryption later. Unlike Y2K, which had a definitive date associated wth the risk, the timing of a capable quantum attack remains uncertain. As such, migration planning is sensible now, independent of IBM’s application and hardware milestones.

The following competitive signals are seen in the Qualitate data and are almost exclusively security-related:

The opportunity for specialists also remains open. One participant states:

“The field is still not crystallized. And probably we will not necessarily rely on the hyperscalers. Probably will rely on specialists.” – Global head of analytics, financial services and insurance, large U.S. corporation (Source: Qualitate)

Our take is that technical credibility and existing relationships, combined with the ability to affect a successful migration, may all influence these purchases. IBM has many assets, but customers are still evaluating alternatives. Success in quantum-safe security strengthens its commercial position without, by itself, resolving which quantum computing architecture or application platform will prevail when quantum goes mainstream.

Quantum computing also needs to progress from building exceptional devices to producing dependable systems repeatedly. The manufacturing announcements around IBM’s roadmap deserve scrutiny in that context.

In September, IBM acquired, Anderon, finalizing a $1 billion CHIPS award supported by an additional $1 billion IBM investment. IBM has reported it has an Albany, New York-based, 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry serving customers across the ecosystem, with initial wafers already running through the facility.

Our view is that the learning curve will be as important as any single milestone. More repeatable production can confer experience advantages to IBM (Wright’s Law), much in the same way Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has demonstrated its leadership in semiconductor manufacturing. Serving multiple customers could help support volume across shared infrastructure. Whether those benefits emerge depends on demand, process stability, yields and the ability to protect each customer’s intellectual property. In addition, IBM can learn from Intel’s missteps and its own foundry challenges.

The industry needs to watch for manufacturing progress alongside qubit performance. Capital investments are followed by innovation. IBM’s August acquisition of HRL Laboratories adds a related strategic chess move. The rationale explained by IBM is to acquire expertise in silicon-spin qubits, sensing, materials, cryogenics, controls, packaging and interconnects. IBM describes that expertise as complementary to its superconducting work and identifies opportunities to collaborate with Anderon.

We interpret the acquisition as a way for IBM to control its destiny in a return to its vertically integrated mainframe past. At the same time, it doesn’t have the volume economics to achieve its objectives purely as a captive/integrated systems player. So it must open up its manufacturing capability to other parties, including its competitors.

Taken together, the public announcements at QDC26 suggest a broader platform ambition. IBM is connecting access to quantum hardware and software with classical computing, application functions, development tools and the like. We believe this could increase its role in the customer’s research process and create more opportunities for ecosystem partners to package specialized capabilities.

The competitive advantage will come from making useful work easier to perform and repeat. A customer that can move from a scientific experiment to a reliable result at scale, with less effort, has a reason to stay with a vendor and invest more. That advantage still has to be earned through application quality, performance, service reliability and superior economics.

There is also a customer tradeoff – the classic lock-in risk. An integrated service can reduce operational complexity while increasing dependence on the provider’s tooling and ecosystem. Open-source tools help minimize the risk, but portability also depends on whether models, workflows, validation and operational models transfer to another platform. Our spring conversations with Kranzlmüller – and his emphasis on technological independence – along with Shehata’s interest in interoperable specifications – make that point clear.

We would not declare IBM as a decisive winner from this conference. But the company has presented an impressive combination of hardware, software and infrastructure progress. Customers will determine its value through repeated use and outcomes. Competing systems from specialists and hyperscalers – as well as progress from classical methods – will continue to shape the narrative.

If Jay Gambetta’s prediction holds true, the next two years will produce a more tangible conversation around industry impact. Look for significantly more quantum POCs, more named customers solving consequential problems and a measurable change in a scientific or business decision. We would also want enough evidence for an independent team to assess the contribution; and for the customer to explain the full cost of achieving an outcome.

For enterprise leaders, the sensible approach is to separate cryptographic readiness from quantum application programs tied to specific problems and economics.

IBM has made a stronger case that the surrounding machinery for useful quantum computing is coming together. The future test is whether customers can show what changed because of quantum. A demonstrably improved scientific result or an economically superior workflow would make the 2028 ambition impressive.

That is the evidence we will be watching.

What’s on your quantum radar? Let us know.

#5709. Another Promising Study on Statins in Compensated Cirrhosis

— There are no approved treatments to prevent hepatic decompensation

Statin initiation among adults with compensated cirrhosis was associated with a lower risk of hepatic decompensation and lower overall mortality, according to a large observational study.

Among over 18,000 patients, the cumulative incidence of hepatic decompensation was 18.2% for those who took statins versus 22.7% for those who didn't take statins (adjusted subhazard ratio [aSHR] 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.96, P=0.008), reported Monica Tincopa, MD, of the University of California San Diego, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

The cumulative incidence of overall mortality was 14.6% for statin users compared with 21.2% for non-users (aSHR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.87, P<0.001).

Over 5 years, the number needed to treat to prevent one episode of decompensation was 25, a number that dropped to 21 over 8 years.

"Decompensation really is the turning point in cirrhosis," Tincopa said. Without approved treatments to prevent decompensation, "current options are really limited to treating the underlying causes of liver disease."

Statins offer potential anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic benefits in cirrhosis, as well as reductions in hepatic portal vein pressure. However, research on statins and decompensation prevention has delivered "highly conflicting" results, Tincopa noted.

Other observational studies have suggested that statin use is associated with lower risks of decompensation and death, including research in veterans with hepatitis C-related compensated cirrhosis. But randomized trials have shown unfavorable results. Ongoing studies such as the phase III SACRED trial of simvastatin in patients with high-risk compensated cirrhosis could bring greater clarity.

The current study included adults with cirrhosis and no prior hepatic decompensation, as determined by ICD-10 codes. Patients with liver transplant or HIV were excluded. The investigators analyzed electronic health record data from the University of California Health Data Warehouse on patients seen at affiliated health facilities from 2012 to 2026.

Statin users and non-users had to have no statin in the 90 days after a cirrhosis diagnosis. Statin users received a prescription after that 90-day lead-in period and had a 90-day qualifying window in which they had no decompensations or deaths. Follow-up for both groups began at 180 days after a cirrhosis diagnosis.

Median age at cirrhosis diagnosis was 58 years, 44% of patients were women, and 51% were white. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) was the cause of cirrhosis in 73.7% of statin users and 59% of non-users, and the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score was at least 10 in 2.9% of statin users and 9.4% of non-users. Coronary artery disease was present in 17.9% of statin patients and 3.5% of those who didn't take statins.

The median duration of statin exposure was about 2.6 years, and 75% of statins taken were lipophilic. Median follow-up time was 7.9 years after cirrhosis diagnosis.

First decompensation events were lower in statin users versus non-users, including ascites (12.7% vs 17.1%, respectively), hepatic encephalopathy (4.8% vs 6.5%), variceal bleeding (1.4% vs 2.1%), hepatorenal syndrome (0.3% vs 0.7%), and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (0.2% vs 0.6%).

Limitations included potential residual confounding and the use of ICD-10 codes to determine cirrhosis and outcomes. The study also didn't assess statin doses or formulations.

#5708. Managing Offshore Wind in the Face of Uncertainty

This report lays out key adaptive management principles and recommendations for regulators.

Despite current headwinds from the Trump administration, offshore wind energy is essential for transitioning away from harmful fossil fuels to a clean energy economy. Offshore wind could provide more than three times the electricity required to power the United States, giving the country an opportunity to fight climate change, reduce local and regional air and water pollution, and grow a new industry that supports thousands of high-quality careers.

While the need for clean energy is urgent, we can and must ensure that all offshore wind in the United States, including floating offshore wind systems, are developed responsibly and in a manner that avoids, minimizes, mitigates, and monitors for adverse impacts to biodiversity and coastal and marine ecosystems. “Adaptive management” is crucial for meeting the dual goals of facilitating a rapid transition to renewable energy while minimizing impacts to the ocean in the face of uncertainty—and continuing to do so over time.

This report explores how adaptive management can be implemented in offshore wind development, provides examples of its use in other energy sectors today, and offers clear recommendations for agencies and policymakers.

#5707. Florida Sinks SS United States In Gulf Of Mexico To Protect The Environment, And I'm Sorry, But That's Just Too Many Jokes

In a hilariously ironic turn of events, Okaloosa County, Florida, sank the SS United States to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico on Veteran's Day, turning it into the world's largest artificial reef to provide shelter for local marine life in the wake of human-caused coral reef decimation in the area. The SS United States is longer than the Titanic, measuring 990 feet from bow to stern and 17 stories in height. It was once the fastest ocean liner in the world, known for carrying royalty and celebrities between the U.S. and Europe from its maiden voyage in 1952 to its retirement in 1969.

It actually still holds the record for the world's fastest trans-Atlantic ocean liner, accomplishing the trek in 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 35.59 knots, and it achieved top speeds of over 38.3 knots, or 44 mph, during trials. This serves as a reminder that even once-great nations — er, ships — can find themselves fallen so far from their former glory that they are better off being totally gutted and sank to the bottom of the ocean rather than wasting time and resources attempting to resuscitate them only for them to still be outdated and irrelevant in a modern world.

The SS United States was originally designed to be converted from luxury ocean liner to troop transport vessel in the event of war like the also-retired Queen Mary was, with the ability to carry 14,000 troops 10,000 miles without refueling, though the SS United States never actually faced wartime use. It was powered by four Westinghouse 1,000-psi steam turbines and eight boilers, which combined to produce a mind-boggling total power output of 240,000 horsepower.

Following the ship's retirement in 1969, the SS United States, "spent its years haunting old shipyards while failed plans to restore it came and went" according to Northeastern Global News. Okaloosa County bought the vessel in 2024 after it faced a court-ordered eviction from its prior docking point at Pier 82 along the Delaware River in South Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where it stayed for nearly three decades.

Okaloosa County chose to sink the ship in its waters to attract tourism from divers, as its top funnels should be easily accessible at just 55 feet below the surface, while its keel will be at a depth of 180 feet. Prior to this, the largest artificial reef on the planet was the 910-foot-long USS Oriskany, which was a U.S. warship that was intentionally sunk in 2006. The SS United States Conservancy plans to commemorate the remarkable ship by constructing a museum and visitor's center in Florida.

#5706. Advances and Unmet Needs in Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease

— It's better care that has led to better survival, not new treatment options

As the 1970s came to a close, sickle cell disease (SCD) remained largely a pediatric condition because few children born in the U.S. with the condition survived to adulthood. Today, about 95% of children born with SCD in developed nations survive to adulthood. Median life expectancy in the U.S. has reached 60 years, meaning half of all patients live to that age, as compared with less than 40% just 10 years ago.

The dramatic improvement in survival evolved from an amalgamation of factors including universal screening of newborns, prophylactic penicillin to prevent bacterial infections, immunization against Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and broader and better-informed use of FDA-approved therapies for SCD. A recent multi-article review covered some of the key developments, as well as ongoing challenges and unmet needs.

Ironically, a clinical trial that did not meet its primary endpoint has profoundly influenced management of SCD. The randomized, placebo-controlled BABY HUG trial failed to show that hydroxyurea reduced the risk of kidney and spleen damage by 50% in very young children with SCD. Nonetheless, the trial showed that patients randomized to hydroxyurea had significantly fewer SCD-associated clinical events, including pain, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, blood transfusion, and hospitalization. Investigators concluded that hydroxyurea "can now be considered for all very young children with sickle cell anemia."

BABY HUG was a landmark clinical trial because of the history of hydroxyurea, which was initially approved only for adults with SCD who met specific high-risk criteria. Published more than a decade ago, the trial established clinical principles that remain highly relevant today for children with SCD.

"[BABY HUG] gave us the evidence that hydroxyurea can be used as prevention, so before kids start having all these complications," Allison King, MD, MPH, PhD, of Washington University in St. Louis, told MedPage Today. "BABY HUG was really helpful because instead of being so reactive, the practice could be very proactive in pediatrics."

A recent analysis of more than 2,000 children with sickle cell anemia treated with hydroxyurea established long-term safety and efficacy. Children followed for as long as 8 years had significantly fewer and briefer hospitalizations, and laboratory data showed sustained improvement in hemoglobin in patients with good treatment adherence.

The Silent Cerebral Infarct Transfusion trial, published more than a decade ago, also had a transformative impact on SCD management. The results, in 200 children with sickle cell anemia, showed that regular blood transfusions significantly reduced the risk of silent cerebral infarction, which can have more subtle neurologic effects as compared with a stroke.

"A lot of our kids, and adults, have cognitive deficits, which are kind of like invisible disabilities because [the patients] can be quite verbal but have significant attention problems, processing speed, executive function that limit their ability to progress in their daily activities," said King. "Also, silent infarcts are a high risk for having overt strokes. Now it's an evidence-based guideline that we should be screening, as well as responding and transfusing, to prevent the progression."

Fast forward a decade and gene therapy became the next transformative clinical development in SCD, offering the potential for cure. Unfortunately, other therapeutic options for SCD have remained limited throughout the decade. One of the approved drugs, voxelotor (Oxbryta), was withdrawn from the market after post-approval data analysis and real-world clinical experience showed the benefits no longer outweighed the risks. Concern has arisen about the future status of another approved agent, crizanlizumab (Adakveo), which lost its conditional European marketing approval. Additionally, the drug failed to outperform placebo for reducing episodes of vaso-occlusive crisis in a recent phase III trial.

Moreover, cost and access remain major obstacles to expansion of gene therapy as a treatment option. In 2025, fewer than 200 patients worldwide received the two gene therapies, which come with a hefty price tag of $2-$3 million. Additionally, the process for screening and preparing patients for gene therapy can be "laborious" for many families, said King.

Despite the advances, more and more effective therapies are an ongoing need for patients with SCD, said Ofelia Alvarez, MD, of the University of Miami Health System.

"There is still a lot to do," she told MedPage Today. "The most widely used medication, hydroxyurea, does not work for all children with sickle cell anemia. Some patients do not respond. They continue to have low hemoglobin despite the treatment. We need new therapies to improve anemia, to decrease complications. They are always in need."

Better transitional care also has contributed to better survival in SCD. However, the quality of care and the ability to provide good transitional care vary greatly. Transition involves much more than handing off a patient from pediatric care to adult care, said Alvarez. Most young patients need to be educated about the disease itself, what medications are available and how they are used, and how to make appointments. Some need to learn about practical issues, such as budgeting, transportation, and learning to live independently.

"Here at the University of Miami, we have a very robust program that is co-created with patients and explained to the parents," said Alvarez. "After the transition, we follow up with the patients to see how they feel about the process and whether they have become integrated into the [adult] practice... . I personally don't have a lot of problems because I work very closely with the adult providers."

In some settings and circumstances, transition into adult care can be complicated and anything but a smooth process. The age at transition varies from practice to practice, but 18 is a common age. King, who specializes in caring for children, has expanded her patient age range up to 26. She described a 23-year-old patient whose circumstances are not rare in the SCD community.

"He has been intermittently homeless for 2 years," said King. "In his words, he 'couch surfs.' He doesn't have a stable place to live. He's not sure where he's getting his food. His meds are always being stolen, so he's frequently in the hospital for pain."

The case also illustrates the problem with using pain as a patient-reported endpoint for judging treatment efficacy, which has been a historical standard for the FDA.

"Pain is so multifactorial," said King. "It could be just sickling, and I'm not trying to minimize that, but it could be very biologically driven, but often, particularly in older teens and adults, psychosocial factors really are big drivers. That makes it difficult to tease out what's really driving a patient's pain."

Finding the origin of a patient's pain has been complicated by the fact that "for the last 20 years, we were sort of crawling our way out of the opioid crisis," said Jeffrey Glassberg, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"When I was in med school, we were taught that there was no danger to opioids," Glassberg told MedPage Today. "If you're treating pain, no harm could come to the patient. Today, I think most people who treat a lot of sickle cell patients would agree: Opioids cause pain. Full stop."

"We have noted that the more opioids that we were giving over the last couple of decades, the more pain our patients would experience, and that pain is non-vaso-occlusive," he continued. "Our latest research is really finding that patients feel that the pain is identical to vaso-occlusive crisis ... The more opioids you give, the more pain that patients will experience that's non-vaso-occlusive, but feels the same."

A number of candidate drugs for SCD have failed to pass muster with the FDA because they did not show a reduction in vaso-occlusive crises. Moving away from that as an endpoint for efficacy and toward a more objective endpoint -- such as organ damage -- might increase the likelihood of more drug approvals and more treatment options for patients, said Glassberg.

#5705. Data Centers, AI, & the Growing Demand for Energy: Impacts, Risks, & Solutions

Learn how the rapid growth of data centers is affecting electricity bills, public health, communities, and the environment and what can be done about it.

Data centers, the physical infrastructure powering the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and our increasingly digital lives, are expanding at an unprecedented pace and scale around the world. This growth is creating enormous new demand for electricity and other resources, with consequences for communities and the environment. In the United States, where data center development is surging, unchecked growth could raise electricity bills for families and small businesses, strain power grids and water supplies, increase pollution, and slow progress toward a clean energy future.

Communities should not be left to bear the costs of this expansion without a meaningful voice in the decisions that affect them. People deserve transparency and a real say in whether and how data centers are built. The wealthy technology companies driving this growth should pay for the infrastructure their facilities require rather than shifting those costs onto the public, bring new clean energy to meet new electricity demand, and meet strong protections for public health and the environment.

Linked below are fact sheets, expert blogs, guides, and other resources that explore the impacts of data center development in the United States and around the world as well as solutions that can help ensure people and the planet remain at the center of the decisions ahead.

Asking ChatGPT a quick question might feel innocuous, but you might end up paying for it in the long run. The massive data centers that are popping up around the country to support the AI boom are using up enormous amounts of energy and water and creating noise and air pollution. NRDC’s Ben Schaefer, senior manager of strategic communications, and Jackson Morris, director of state power sector policy, dive into how these centers can impact nearby communities and your energy bill.
