#5693. Michelle Yeoh Says Window Seats Are Underrated, And She's Right (That You Should Leave The Aisle Seats For Me)

By definition, hot takes are supposed to be controversial. If everyone agrees with your hot take, it's probably a lukewarm take at best, because that's how kids decided the slang worked. Kareem Rahma has taken advantage of this with Subway Takes, a show where he sits on the New York subway and records people's hot takes. This week, Oscar-winning actress Michelle Yeoh made an appearance and decided the hill she would die on is that window seats are underrated. A lot of people won't like it, but you know what? She's right.

Flying is a miracle of engineering and modern manufacturing. We literally built machines that defy the will of the gods, zoom across our skies, and let us travel in ways we were never meant to travel. Should I have been able to pull off a whirlwind visit to Boston while living in Georgia? Probably not, but the miracle of flight made it possible, and there's always going to be some thing special about sitting in a window seat that lets you see the beautiful world beneath you. Los Angeles isn't the prettiest city in the world, but even LA looks incredible from 10,000 or 15,000 feet.

With the window seat, you'll also have an easier time napping on your flight, and air travel takes so much time out of your day, you could probably use a snooze. Yes, most seats now have those bendy headrests that are supposed to make napping a little easier, but nothing beats using a sweater as a pillow and leaning against the plane. The bendy headrests can try, but while they're better than nothing, they still don't work all that great. All humans need to sleep, so book a window seat, enjoy the view, and then take a nice nap once the plane makes it above the clouds.

Does going to the bathroom get a little awkward? Sure, but there's no reason you have to drink four whiskey cokes before you board your flight. They have edibles for that now. Any time you get up to go to the bathroom, that's also the opportunity to make a new friend. Most importantly, if everyone who reads this ends up fighting over those beautiful views from the window, there will be more aisle seats available for me to take. Michelle may have a point, but I still prefer the aisle and will not be changing my mind.

#5692. Hydropower Generation in the Southwest Fell to Record Lows This Summer

Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows.

However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years.

We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won’t eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity.

According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region’s generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.

#5690. 32 Hospitalized After Asphalt Tanker Slams Into And Sinks Docked Riverboat In New Orleans

The Mississippi River is partially closed after a tanker ship t-boned and sank a docked riverboat with approximately 129 passengers and crew members on board in the Port of New Orleans at approximately 12:30 p.m. ET on Friday. City officials said an estimated 32 people have been transported to nearby hospitals with non-critical injuries, and all passengers are now accounted for, miraculously confirming no casualties from the tragedy. The exact number of injuries caused in the collision is not currently known, as it remains an active and evolving incident. The collision happened outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, and the U.S. Coast Guard closed the Mississippi River to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96.

The American Cruise Lines' American Heritage riverboat was docked for about two hours to begin passenger disembarkation when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with it. WDSU News said, "Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel are on scene, conducting rescue and response operations." Their rapid response is being called "a miracle on the Mississippi."

Louisiana Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser told ABC News he was worried about the victims because these type of river cruises tend to draw elderly passengers. WDSU said rescued passengers are being brought into the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and assistance. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said the water temperature near the shipwreck is about 66 degrees, which is cold enough to potentially cause hypothermia if a person is exposed to it for too long.

There is no confirmed cause of the crash, though it is suspected to be due to a loss of steering. After the initial impact, the riverboat began taking on water and capsized very rapidly, and it is now resting on its side at the dock. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry rushed to the scene and said he spoke with President Donald Trump about the crash, who told him he had any support he needed. The U.S. Coast Guard is now working on reopening the river, and it is working with salvage assistance teams to salvage the vessel and remove it from the area.

#5689. 10 Reasons for the Big Blue Wave

I wrote the other day about a top reason US voters said they voted for Democrats in such large numbers — corruption in the Trump household, Trump administration, and Republican Party. It was surprising to me that this showed up as the biggest factor for so many people … even though it was also a huge one for me. However, I think everyone knows what the most significant reason was for the dramatic, historic shift in voting. It’s the economy, stupid! That’s the famous old quote from James Carville, a political strategist working for Bill Clinton when he was running for president in 1992, and it’s as relevant as ever. With that in mind, let’s take a look at some of the top reasons for the Big Blue Wave.

Inflation has hit and hit and hit. Donald Trump said while campaigning for president in 2024, “Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again.” However, of course, beyond the fact that he didn’t come close to doing that and was just making an obviously false promise, Trump actually jacked up inflation significantly with his obsessive, high tariffs and with his war on Iran. Whereas it’s often hard to tie inflation to a specific presidential policy, in this case, we had two specific presidential policies that clearly caused inflation! Even when there are no clear links, voters blame the president for such matters, so imagine how much they must have done so in this case!

Aside from inflation, the economy overall isn’t great. The country isn’t adding a bunch of jobs, wages and salaries aren’t rising much, and people by and large don’t feel optimistic about their financial futures. So, combined with quickly rising costs, a very meh economy had voters wanting change.

As already discussed at length, voters were fed up with corruption in the Republican Party. As some CleanTechnica readers pointed out, if people were prospering financially and not being hit with severe inflation, many of them probably wouldn’t care about the corruption. However, when considering #1 and #2, people naturally get quite frustrated with blatant corruption and essentially high-volume robbery from Donald Trump, the Trump family, Trump staffers, and the Republican Party broadly.

Naturally, this is heavily linked to #1, since it is largely this war that has led to gas prices rising so much. However, also more broadly, Americans are fed up with forever wars in the Middle East, there’s never been a good and strong case for why Trump started this war (as tends to be the case with these wars in the Middle East), and many people really don’t like seeing innocent schoolchildren being bombed to death. Trump was supposed to be an anti-war president (I know that many people believed that, even though Trump is a naturally aggressive, violent person who seemed to me like someone who would obviously get into wars). Voters who cared a lot about this topic might have felt betrayed by Trump and swung strongly away from him and the Republican Party (which has a tendency to get us into these oil wars in the Middle East).

Even for many people who thought we needed stronger actions to stop people from coming to the United States, the inhumane, deadly, Gestapo-like ICE army — often including violent people with their faces covered and without ID acting like the mafia — was a step or ten too far. There are countless stories of good, innocent people being jailed without cause, or even murdered, by this Nazi-like police force. There was clearly a huge blue shift in certain places as a result of this.

Many voters have gotten extremely concerned about Republicans under Trump’s leadership eroding the foundations of our democracy. While this became a major problem in Trump’s first term, he has gone much further in his second term. Apparently, more people have woken up to this problem and it has freaked them out.

A massive rollout of AI and data centers — often feeling completely forced on us — has upset a lot of Americans. This does come back to #1, too. Giant data centers have jacked up electricity prices a ton in several regions. Others are threatened with the same thing happening. The same thing has also happened from the crypto craze, which more and more people have also found to be a scam. Seeing billions upon billions trillions of dollars funneled toward AI companies while people are struggling, and then seeing electricity prices rising significantly — surprise, surprise — pisses people off and makes them vote for change.

No matter how you cut it, people vote based on money — in particular, their own money. Whether it’s food prices, gas prices, electricity prices, clothing prices, doll prices, computer prices, car prices, or other prices, people don’t like it when they have to pay a lot more money for stuff — especially when they aren’t making much more money, or more money at all. Simply put, this matter deserves extra weight, because the critical thing swing voters are often voting on is just that — money.

Of course, there are solar, wind, and EV aspects to all of this. Trump has made the US spend a fortune to stop wind and solar farms from providing the US with cheap electricity, and he has made the US spend a fortune keeping old, dirty coal power plants open. High gas prices have also pushed people to buy electric cars, but mostly in other countries where there’s more EV choice and more people have more sense on this topic. However, by and large, I don’t think American voters really shifted much based on Trump stopping renewable energy projects, promoting coal and gas, or limiting EV choice in the United States. People voting for Democrats on climate and cleantech matters were already voting for Democrats based on these issues. It’s unlikely many people at all shifted from red to blue because of these factors.

#5688. 4 insights from Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026: AI agents join the team as working colleagues

At Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026, AI agents moved out of single-player chat windows and into shared workspaces. There they work beside people as named, auditable members of the team. Block Inc. built these tools to run itself as an intelligence company, and it is now offering them to other businesses, building on Buzz, its open-source workspace for humans and AI agents. Block introduced Builderlab as a set of tools for teams and AI agents to work together.

The next phase will depend less on how capable a single agent becomes than on how well agents collaborate, share an organization’s context and stay inside firm security boundaries. Block plans to spread that model with open-source code, model-agnostic design and hosted infrastructure. The company is making that push while its core business delivers a third straight guidance raise.

“If you’re talking about making the whole organization more productive, you need to break down these distinctions between what the software does and what the people do,” said Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

Alison Kosik (left) and co-host Gillin spoke with industry experts during Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026 in San Francisco. The interviews covered Block’s open-source business model, agents with their own identities, the shift from prompting to overnight delegation and the security controls that let enterprises trust autonomous systems. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are four standout insights from the event:

Builderlab gives developers endlessly customizable agents on an open-source plug-in architecture, and the launch audience of application builders cheered the idea, according to Gillin. Agents in Buzz have names, avatars and personalities. That shifts the focus from switching among software-as-a-service applications to the work itself, and it could threaten SaaS companies. The revenue model follows the classic open-source pattern of giving the software away and charging for the convenience of a hosted cloud service, he explained. Block said little about commercialization or about Cash App, which brings in 60% of its revenue, according to Gillin.

Most AI tools are built for one person at a time, so each user becomes the bottleneck when results have to be shared with a team, noted Lucas Isaza, product lead of Buzz at Block. In Buzz, agents have their own identities, can be tagged like colleagues and leave an audit trail of every action. Plug-ins, added after the first version launched in July, let anyone reshape the interface. Nontechnical staff, such as account managers building personal dashboards, have been the heaviest users of the companion apps platform. Companies can self-host the open-source code, use a free tier or add funds for remote agents, models and extra storage, Isaza highlighted.

Builderlab sits as an interface layer above the models, so Buzz can use agents from any AI lab and switch to the newest frontier model as it arrives, emphasized Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block. Remote agents run in central cloud environments that are easier to secure than laptops. People can hand them large assignments overnight and act as reviewers. Instead of soft guardrails, agents run on secure building blocks that never grant them permission for certain actions. Some teams have shipped software releases 50% to 75% faster. Axen expects agents to need much less human steering within the next year because they already sit inside the conversation.

Securing agents that act on their own does not mean starting over, because principles such as least privilege, isolated environments and egress controls still apply, shared James Nettesheim, chief information security officer and head of enterprise technology at Block. Builderlab gives every agent a full identity owned by a human, runs it in hardened cloud virtual machines and records its actions in a cryptographically signed ledger that cannot be altered. Block is also building information flow control, which tags data from sensitive sources so the security policy travels with that data and blocks leaks. AI already reviews Block’s code and sorts its security alerts. Nettesheim added that agents let defenders keep pace with attackers’ machine speed.

#5687. Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs

This analysis of eight residential programs shows that, if properly implemented, cities can use a new organics collection program to build a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

Residential curbside organics collection is expanding across the United States as states and local governments seek to reduce food waste sent to landfills and incinerators, meet waste diversion and climate goals, and respond to landfill capacity constraints. Yet for many communities, the perceived cost of adding organics recycling collection atop existing trash and recycling collection remains a significant barrier to implementation.

NRDC’s Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report finds that there is no single predetermined cost of implementing and operating an organics collection program. The cost to communities depends substantially on how organics collection is designed and, critically, how it is integrated into the broader solid waste system. A municipality that simply adds weekly organics collection to an otherwise unchanged garbage and recycling program is likely to see an increase in cost. However, a municipality that uses the introduction of organics to evaluate and optimize collection frequency, routes, contracts, processing arrangements, participation, and funding can offset a significant portion of the new service cost. In fact, with deliberate planning and system-wide optimization, curbside organics can serve not simply as an added service but as a catalyst for a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

This analysis draws on eight established residential curbside organics programs and two active pilot programs representing communities of different sizes, densities, regions, service models, and participation structures. Across these communities, several findings emerge:

The community comparisons demonstrate the practical significance of these choices. In several communities that were studied, residents receive garbage, recycling, and organics collection at rates that are comparable to what residents in peer communities pay for garbage and recycling alone. For example, in Austin, Texas, residents pay approximately $29 per month for three-stream curbside service, compared with approximately $22 per month for garbage and recycling service in Raleigh, North Carolina. The comparison is not intended to suggest that every community can replicate a particular rate; rather, it demonstrates that the addition of organics does not necessarily translate into a proportionate increase in the total cost of residential solid waste service.

The Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report aims to support states and local communities in implementing effective strategies to fund residential curbside organic waste collection programs as a critical tool to improving resilience, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and diverting material from landfills and incinerators. The central implication for local governments is therefore straightforward: The affordability of curbside organics is largely a program design question. Communities considering organics collection can begin by evaluating the economics and performance of their existing solid waste system; identifying efficiencies that can help offset the new service; testing critical assumptions through a pilot, where appropriate; and finally, designing a full-scale program around the participation, collection, processing, and funding structures that best fit local conditions. To support this process, the report translates these findings into a three-phase implementation framework for evaluating the existing system, designing and testing an organics program, and moving toward financially sustainable full-scale implementation.

#5686. Prescriptions Down 25%, Overdoses Cut in Half: What Stopped a Gabapentinoid Surge?

— Study identifies three interventions that may have influenced pregabalin use

High-profile media coverage of the harms associated with the gabapentinoid pregabalin (Lyrica) and tighter safeguards coincided with fewer prescriptions and overdoses in Australia, a retrospective study showed.

Following a media campaign, tighter dispensing rules, and boxed warnings, pregabalin prescriptions and overdoses dropped significantly below projected trends -- falling by 25% and 47%, respectively -- reported Rose Cairns, PhD, of the University of Sydney, and co-authors in The BMJ.

This was a reversal from a steep upward trajectory that had persisted since 2013, the researchers noted. The shift corresponded to ongoing monthly reductions in prescriptions of 0.7% (95% CI 0.5-0.9) and in poison center overdose calls of 1.6% (95% 1.0-2.3).

Australia historically has had a big problem with pregabalin use and overdose, and many other countries face similar issues, Cairns noted.

"Importantly, the interventions that were associated with a decrease in harms included things like raising public awareness of the risks via the media and boxed warnings. These relatively 'soft' interventions can still have an impact," she told MedPage Today.

The findings are "really positive, but we think use of pregabalin is still far too high," Cairns continued. "There's a lot of off-label use for conditions with minimal evidence to back that up. And while high-risk use has decreased, we really need to continue to minimize co-use with opioids, which has been shown to increase the risk of death."

Gabapentinoids -- pregabalin and gabapentin -- were originally developed as antiseizure drugs. Subsequent indications have expanded to include neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and fibromyalgia.

"Despite this relatively narrow range of approved indications, gabapentinoids are considered 'blockbuster' drugs," Cairns and colleagues wrote. "High-income countries have the highest rates of gabapentinoid consumption, while low- and middle-income countries have had the highest consumption growth in recent years. Most of this consumption is driven by off-label use for non-registered indications."

In the U.S., pregabalin is scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act. Gabapentin is not scheduled at the federal level but eight states have enacted legislation to classify gabapentin as a schedule V controlled substance.

In 2019, the FDA warned that respiratory depression or death may occur in patients taking pregabalin or gabapentin with opioid pain medicines or other drugs that depress the central nervous system. Despite this, co-prescribing of gabapentinoids and opioids persists.

In the U.K., one-third of substance use deaths involve a gabapentinoid, predominantly pregabalin, and deaths involving gabapentinoids have more than doubled from 2018 to 2022, Cairns and co-authors noted.

The study in Australia is "timely and rigorous, but these figures warrant caution," noted David Juurlink, MD, PhD, of the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto, in an accompanying editorial. "The ecological design cannot establish causation, and poison center calls are an imperfect measure of poisoning incidence, influenced by reporting practices and patterns of healthcare use," he pointed out.

Pregabalin should be used more selectively, Juurlink argued. "Although it can provide meaningful relief in some patients with neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia, most do not achieve substantial pain relief," he wrote.

"For other painful conditions, the evidence is even less encouraging," Juurlink added. "Randomized trials and meta-analyses have found no convincing evidence of benefit for low back pain or sciatica, conditions for which the drug is nevertheless frequently prescribed. Pregabalin's commercial success, in other words, has far outstripped its demonstrated clinical utility."

To evaluate pregabalin use and misuse in Australia, Cairns and colleagues evaluated dispensing claims and poison center overdose data from 2016 to 2024, focusing on three key events: widespread media reporting about the harms of pregabalin in December 2018, tighter prescribing restrictions after April 2020, and the introduction of boxed warnings in February 2021.

The researchers randomly sampled 10% of Australians with drug subsidies and 50% of calls placed to the country's largest poison control center. During the study period, 227,864 people were dispensed 3,441,851 pregabalin prescriptions, and 4,871 pregabalin overdose calls were reported.

Use and overdoses peaked in 2018 before plateauing and declining. Dispensing dropped significantly at three time points: in December 2018 (corresponding to high-profile press coverage), in May 2020 (after tighter prescribing restrictions were introduced), and in December 2021 (after boxed warnings were in effect).

The findings are observational, the researchers acknowledged. The study analyzed subsidized prescriptions only and poisons center data may be subject to reporting bias, they added. The researchers also could not determine patients' access to pain treatments.

Back in the day, the Challenger had a starting price of $2,850, whereas the more potent R/T went for $3,266.

#5684. Who Can Weather the Health Storm?

States facing the greatest health damage from climate change are the least equipped to protect their residents.

Across the United States, climate change is intensifying extreme weather events, resulting in escalating public health harms and severe economic damage. For example, devastating inland flooding in Texas in 2025 killed 134 people and damaged $1 billion worth of residential property; 2025’s catastrophic wildfires in Southern California destroyed more than 10,000 buildings (at a cost of $63 billion) and triggered more than 8,000 health-care visits; and Hurricane Milton’s 2024 landfall in Florida killed 32 people and damaged $34 billion in property. These climate costs are typically borne by disaster victims, insurers, state agencies, and the federal government. Given the retreat of federal leadership from climate policy, state governments are increasingly looking to improve preparedness and resiliency in order to reduce future costs and health impacts.

However, a new analysis led by NRDC and published in the journal Health Affairs sheds light on key state-level gaps between climate change–linked health damage and levels of preparedness. We find that some of the most climate-burdened states are the least equipped to help their residents recover from climate disasters and prepare for future dangers. The intersection of escalating climate risks and adaptation vulnerabilities demands state policy intervention. Better integrating social protection policies into state climate resiliency plans can help states close these gaps and better safeguard their residents.

#5682. Bandit Tow Companies Are Scamming People In California And Beyond

Getting in a car crash can be stressful enough, and even if no one's injured, your bank account can still feel the pain. But it's not just paying for repairs that can be expensive. The wrecker that conveniently comes along to haul your vehicle away can cost you plenty as well. In fact, that's what bandit towing companies are all about. They prey on accident victims by arriving unsolicited and using high-pressure tactics to get vulnerable drivers to agree to a tow. Next, they essentially hold those rides for ransom through outlandish fees and sky-high charges.

In one especially egregious case, Los Angeles police discovered a bandit towing company running an elaborate scam. One person would first claim to be a crash witness at the scene. The "witness" would claim to have video evidence of the accident and offer to text it to the driver involved. Once the driver passed over their digits, though, someone else would call pretending to be from their insurance company and telling them to use the scammer's truck when it showed up. It all seemed legit right up until the hapless drivers tried to get their vehicles back from those folks. In the LA example, police eventually found about 145 cars that had been illegally impounded. It was yet another case of a towing company ignoring laws meant to help people.

Nor is bandit towing limited to the West Coast. Windy City Jalopniks may be aware of Lincoln Towing Service — aka the Lincoln Park Pirates — a towing company so infamous a 1972 folk song was written about it. More recently, the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) reported that predatory towing claims jumped 89% nationwide in the span from 2022 to 2024.

First off, let's be clear: It's illegal in California and other states for a tow truck to roll up to an accident scene uninvited and looking for work. In Michigan, for instance — and subject to a few disclaimers — the state's vehicle code says that "a person shall not travel to the scene of a motor vehicle accident or a disabled vehicle located on public property, property open to the public, or a state trunk line highway and solicit business for a wrecker, recovery, or towing service."

With that in mind, your obvious first step is to stay in control of the situation by only working with a towing company you've contacted yourself. As the NICB puts it, "if you didn't request the tow, say no." The major exception to this rule is if law enforcement needs your vehicle for an investigation. In that case, what happens to the vehicle is up to the authorities. You just have to hope a bad Flock doesn't lead the police to tow the wrong car. Also a good idea: Confirm that the truck that arrives is, in fact, from the service you requested.

Be sure to get all the details about the towing company you can, too, and if at all possible, do not fork over any cash upfront. The NICB notes that "legitimate towing companies" accept checks, credit cards, and other kinds of "traceable payment methods." Here you need to keep in mind that, per the Better Business Bureau, Venmo and similar digital payment services don't really qualify. In the context of consumer protection, paying with these services is basically like paying for cash. Otherwise, we could be seeing you in our next edition of Jalopnik readers' worst tow-truck experiences.

#5681. Major Change to Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines

— ACS now recommends PSA testing every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69

Shifting gears on prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69.

Since the release of its previous guideline 16 years ago, the ACS had recommended that average-risk men consult with a physician before deciding for themselves whether to undergo a screening PSA test.

The new ACS recommendations also strengthened guidelines for men at high risk for prostate cancer, recommending annual screening beginning at age 45 for Black men and those with a strong family history of the disease. The organization previously recommended that those men discuss the pros and cons of screening with a physician at age 40 or 45.

The changes reflect the accumulation of stronger evidence that screening PSA tests reduce prostate cancer mortality and diagnosis of late-stage disease, according to the updated guidelines from Robert Smith, PhD, ACS senior vice president for early cancer detection science, and colleagues, appearing in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians.

"We've just reached a point in our understanding of prostate cancer, especially that [screening] can reduce the risk of being diagnosed with metastatic disease and dying of prostate cancer," Smith told MedPage Today. "We have good protocols for avoiding harms."

Smith noted that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not updated their prostate cancer screening guidelines since 2018. For average-risk men, the USPSTF recommends discussion-backed decisions on PSA testing for men ages 55 to 69.

"I cannot tell you what [their recommendations] would be if they updated them today, but they did not have the data in 2018 that we had in 2025 with the update of the European trial data showing the endurance of the mortality reduction," said Smith.

The update aligns with recent evidence supporting PSA screening for prostate cancer as "one of the most important steps men can take to protect their health," said Ash Tewari, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"We have strong evidence that PSA testing can reduce the risk of dying from prostate cancer, and advances in MRI and other diagnostic tools are helping us identify potentially dangerous cancers while avoiding unnecessary procedures," he said. "Knowing your risk, getting screened regularly, and having these conversations early can save lives."

With the update, the ACS takes a clear position on prostate cancer screening, said Mark Ashamalla, MD, of Episcopal Health Services in New York City.

"For years, the ACS largely focused on encouraging men to discuss the pros and cons of PSA screening with their doctors," said Ashamalla. "Now they're taking a much clearer position and actually recommending regular screening. For men at average risk, that means a PSA blood test every 2 years between ages 50 and 69, while Black men and those with a strong family history should begin annual screening at age 45. This is a significant shift and reflects growing evidence that regular screening can reduce the risk of advanced prostate cancer and save lives."

"The goal isn't to find and treat every prostate cancer," he added. "It's to catch the dangerous ones early enough to make a difference. I think that's the biggest takeaway from these new guidelines."

By way of the guidelines, the ACS also recommends:

The updated guidelines are supportive of the recent trend toward active surveillance as the primary option for men with low-risk prostate cancer.

"It's important to recognize that prostate cancer screening has evolved over the past 30 years," said Smith. "More and more people appreciate that very worrisome harms associated with therapy can be avoided, especially if a man is diagnosed with prostate cancer that is not aggressive. Active treatment should be avoided until such time as it appears that the disease has become aggressive. Some men may be diagnosed with a prostate cancer that's not very aggressive, and they will live with it in that state for the rest of their lives. [They can] avoid harms that are quite diminishing to quality of life."

"On the other hand, if a man's prostate cancer becomes more aggressive, and treatment is necessary, then the process of active surveillance will at least have postponed it for a number of years, allowing men to not have to live with those [treatment-related] side effects," said Smith.

#5680. Tesla Starts Selling Cybercab — $30,000*

Well, it’s a big day in Tesla World. The company has officially launched Cybercab sales. You can now order a Cybercab for the starting price of $30,000 (technically, $29,900). That said, there is an asterisk here — actually, there are two asterisks here. First of all, only people who have been invited to order a Cybercab are able to order one right now — there’s no public ordering page. Secondly, if you do order one, you also need to pay for Full Self Driving — or just “Autonomy” as it’s named on the Tesla webpage. That is listed as $299/month.

So, if you extrapolate $299/month across five years (assuming the price is not going to go up in that time), that’s another $17,940. That would bring your total to $47,840. The $17,940 alone would be more than the cost of the used BMW i3 I recently bought (and for less passenger capacity).

Is nearly $50,000 over five years for a two-seater a good deal? Well, it’s all about that autonomous driving, isn’t it? If you can sit in the car and watch a movie or sleep or work while being driven, the car is clearly going to be worth more than a normal car. If you can send the Cybercab out for taxi services without riding along, it’s clearly worth more than a normal car you have to drive. But, still, is it worth $50,000 across five years? That is the question, and we should find out soon how many people or companies think that’s a good deal.

One important thing to consider, though, is that the car doesn’t come with a steering wheel or pedals (last we’ve heard). That means that once you have the vehicle, you are at the mercy of Tesla and its monthly Autonomy fee. If Tesla decides to raise the fee to $499/month, you presumably have to pay that much or sell the car (or let is sit parked and out of service).

The estimated delivery time for those ordering a Cybercab today is December of this year. You have to pay a $1,000 non-refundable deposit in order to place an order.

So, yes, it is a big, significant day for Tesla. What that ends up meaning, we’ll see….

#5679. The US Navy Will Retire Its Oldest Active Aircraft Carrier After 52 Years Of Service

The oldest aircraft carrier still in service, the USS Nimitz, was commissioned on May 3, 1975, and it's quite something. Measuring approximately 1,092 feet long, it boasts a crew capacity of about 5,000, and — configuration dependent — it can carry up to 90 aircraft. It's essentially a floating air base, so rather than relying on land-based air fields, the U.S. Navy can deploy the Nimitz and operate jets, helicopters, and the like from its deck instead.

Power is sourced from a duo of Westinghouse A4W nuclear reactors, which themselves power four turbines, enabling speed of up to 30 knots. The major benefit of harnessing nuclear power on ships is that it lets them operate for decades before refueling is required. When refueling is required, though, the process takes years to carry out. A major overhaul of the Nimitz, including nuclear refueling, was finished in 2001, but the entire process took the best part of a decade, including planning.

The reason for the ship's retirement now is simple; Nimitz-class carriers were designed with a 50-year service life, and that's been reached. It should really already be tucked up in retirement, but as its replacement, the USS John F. Kennedy, has been delayed, its service has been extended to March 2027. U.S. law dictates that the Navy must keep a minimum of 11 aircraft carriers in service, so the extension of its service was necessary.

The Nimitz hasn't been the longest-serving U.S. aircraft carrier for all that long. In fact, it only took hold of that record in May 2026, pinching the title from the USS Enterprise. Other impressive numbers associated with the aircraft carrier include that in April 2023 it recorded its 350,000th arrested aircraft landing, another record, and it has also played host to more than 200,000 sailors in its time. There'is no denying, it's been a busy ship.

Now that its record-breaking run is coming to an end, questions are being raised about how it can be disassembled and recycled in the most effective, least damaging way possible. However, retirement doesn't mean immediate scrapping. It must be de-armed, safely shut down — including the defueling of its nuclear reactors — and then be prepared for dismantling. First, everything from weapons through to harmful materials, like lead and asbestos, must be carefully removed. Only then — some years down the line, when it's fully inactive and stripped — can disassembly begin.

Its replacement, the USS John F. Kennedy has been a long time coming. We watched it float for the first time seven years ago, and now we're only months away from seeing it officially enter service. The new vessel belongs to the newer Gerald R. Ford class, and it boasts some significant improvements over the Nimitz's now half-century-old design.

Traditional steam-powered catapult-style aircraft launch systems will be replaced with electromagnetic systems, although President Donald Trump has ordered later ships of the same class to revert back to steam catapults. Plus, the new ship sports far more advanced radar and combat systems. It's also far more efficient than the old design, with operations and support costs estimated at $4 billion lower over its life than the costs with Nimitz-class carriers.

The Kennedy's basic size and weight are remarkably similar its predecessor's, though, at 1,092 feet and 100,000 tons. It, too, will use nuclear power, but although its A1B reactors are smaller, they can triple the Nimitz's energy output. Ultimately, the idea is to launch a vessel that can operate aircraft more efficiently, with less maintenance, reduced operational costs, and a higher rate of sorties.

Paris Blockchain Week is now Signal Week, a reflection of cryptocurrency’s global expansion.

“The industry has changed a lot,” said Michael Amar (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week. “We really want to be the place where we bridge traditional finance and digital assets. It’s where the market is finally, and we are embracing it completely. We have the desire to go abroad to launch other conferences. So it made sense that … we join everything under the same roof, but different flows, different marketing and different ticketing.”

Amar and Charlie Meraud (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week, spoke with theCUBE host Gemma Allen, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed what to expect at the 2027 event and the evolution of cryptocurrency. (* Disclosure below.)

#5676. U.S. on the Verge of Forfeiting Major Public Health Victory on Measles

— The nation is having its worst measles year in decades

International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories -- the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus' spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past 2 years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico -- that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.

"It's a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards," said David Margolius, MD, director of Cleveland's health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.

Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

International Health Experts Are Poring Over Measles Data This Week

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for 1 year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.

"It's solely based on genetics," said Amesh Adalja, MD, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have "eliminated" measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.

The CDC Says Loss of Measles Elimination Status Won't Change Its Approach

A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, said this week.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we're working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks," she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and has lauded Trump's executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups' recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

The U.S. Is Having Its Worst Measles Year in Decades

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine -- which is credited with saving millions of lives globally -- is possibly "quite lethal." Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah, and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year -- more than any year in more than three decades -- and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

At Least 50 People Have Died From Measles in Mexico

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed -- in 1963, in the U.S. -- and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.

As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.

#5674. Alzheimer's Study Tracks Faster Tau Buildup in Younger Patients

— Tau spread more rapidly across a wider area of the brain in early-onset Alzheimer's disease

People with early-onset Alzheimer's disease had faster and more severe accumulation of tau than those whose Alzheimer's symptoms started after age 65, imaging data showed.

Compared with older Alzheimer's patients, tau burden was higher in younger patients and spread more rapidly across a wider area of the brain, reported Konstantinos Chiotis, MD, PhD, of the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and co-authors.

Early-onset Alzheimer's patients also had stronger correlations between tau buildup, amyloid-beta accumulation, and broader cognitive decline, Chiotis and colleagues wrote in Science Translational Medicine.

"Younger patients had substantially more tau even after accounting for differences in clinical severity," Chiotis said in a statement. "Their tau also accumulated faster over time. Delayed diagnosis alone does not explain this pattern."

The study compared baseline and longitudinal tau in 390 early-onset Alzheimer's patients with a mean age of 59, and 211 late-onset patients with a mean age of 78. It is the largest to compare tau in both early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease.

"The results confirm that early-onset Alzheimer's disease seems to advance faster both biologically and clinically," Nicolai Franzmeier, PhD, of Ludwig Maximilians University in Munich, who wasn't involved with the study, told MedPage Today. This considerably strengthens previous evidence that linked younger age at symptom onset to more extensive tau pathology, Franzmeier noted.

Early-onset disease accounts for approximately 5% of all Alzheimer's cases, though some studies suggest young-onset forms of Alzheimer's and other dementias may be more common than once thought.

"Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's are more likely than older patients to present with symptoms unrelated to memory, at least initially," co-author Renaud La Joie, PhD, of the University of California San Francisco, said in a statement. "They might have difficulty interpreting what they are seeing despite a normal eye exam. They might struggle with judging distances and may have trouble reading," he added.

"Some patients may experience a decline in language abilities in which they have difficulty retrieving words and following long sentences, although speech remains fluent," La Joie pointed out. "Others may struggle with executive functioning, such as attention, problem-solving, planning, and adapting to changing situations."

It's not clear why early-onset Alzheimer's disease develops, the researchers noted. To compare early- and late-onset Alzheimer's patients, Chiotis and colleagues studied adults with confirmed amyloid pathology, mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, and tau PET measured with 18F-flortaucipir. A subset of participants had follow-up imaging over 2 to 3 years.

Early-onset patients were from the Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study (LEADS) cohort. Late-onset patients were from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) repository.

The early-onset group had a higher proportion of women compared with the late-onset group (55% vs 42%) and more participants diagnosed with dementia at baseline (72% vs 36%). Nearly one in five early-onset patients had a non-amnestic presentation, while 99.25% of late-onset patients had memory problems.

At baseline, the early-onset group had higher amyloid PET binding and more severe impairment across global cognitive measures, including Mini-Mental State Examination and Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes scores. Over time, early-onset patients accumulated tau tangles faster in every region of interest.

"Although early-onset Alzheimer's disease participants also showed higher amyloid-beta PET burden, the differences in amyloid-beta were substantially smaller than those observed in tau PET burden, consistent with neuropathological studies showing greater differences in tau than in amyloid-beta burden between early-onset Alzheimer's disease and late-onset Alzheimer's disease," Chiotis and co-authors noted.

Co-pathologies were not directly assessed in the study, and their contribution to differences between early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease remains uncertain, the researchers acknowledged.

Young-onset dementia patients can have diagnostic delays which may affect employment, financial security, and family needs, and postpone support and care.

"We need greater awareness of Alzheimer's in younger adults and better access to specialist assessment, including tau PET when clinically appropriate," Chiotis said. "These scans show how much tau pathology is present and where it is located, helping us understand unusual symptoms and how far the disease has progressed biologically."

#5673. Kubernetes gets a second act as AI agents turn one prompt into thousands of inference calls

The rise of agentic AI systems is giving Kubernetes, long valued for its reliability and predictability, an unexpected second act.

As AI spending shifts from training models toward serving them and running agents, the open-source community is developing tools to handle the growing volume of inference requests. The orchestration platform was built from the start for dynamic, distributed workloads, which gave fast-growing AI companies a reliable foundation, according to Jonathan Bryce (pictured), executive director of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

“The AI boom has sparked a massive investment and a huge build-out of infrastructure overall,” Bryce said. “Having Kubernetes built from the beginning to handle really dynamic distributed workloads as those companies were growing like crazy — they had a really reliable, solid foundation to build on at the same time.”

Bryce spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how CNCF projects can meet rising inference demand, make better use of data center hardware and secure AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

New models grab headlines with benchmark scores in math and software engineering. But a model has no value until it can be served at high performance, and early chatbots made that look simple because each message triggered a single inference call, Bryce explained. Agents can make repeated inference calls to complete a single task, a shift the CNCF has put on the KubeCon agenda with its new AI inference and agentic track.

“We’re using coding agents to say, ‘Build me a system that does this,’ and it’ll spawn 10 sub-agents,” Bryce said. “Each of those are doing thousands of inference calls over the course of hours and just churning away.”

As inference demand fuels a data center construction boom and raises local concerns about resource use, the llm-d inference engine and Agent Substrate, which offers compact hosting for long-running agents, aim to get more performance out of existing hardware, Bryce said. Security and control pose another challenge because agents can make different choices when given the same task. OpenShell, a security project now under the CNCF’s neutral governance following Nvidia Corp.’s contribution, drew more than 300 contributing companies within months, a milestone which might once have taken two years to reach, he added.

“What I am constantly thinking about is, ‘How do we lower friction to collaboration?'” Bryce said. “How do we enable people to be able to move at the pace that the world and the industry is moving at, and how do we, while doing that, continue to drive that into collaboration around open solutions that can become those base and infrastructure components that we can all build on?”

#5671. Trial on Statins for Cirrhosis Won't End Debate Anytime Soon

— Phase III study on simvastatin to prevent hepatic decompensation comes up just short

Statin therapy delivered a statistical near miss at lowering risks of hepatic decompensation and liver cancer in patients with compensated cirrhosis, the phase III SACRED trial showed.

In an intention-to-treat analysis, 8.97% of patients who took simvastatin daily for up to 2 years developed ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage, or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) compared with 18.75% of those who received placebo (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.16-1.05, P=0.064), a difference just short of significant.

Overall survival rates also didn't differ significantly between the statin and placebo groups (HR 2.31, 95% CI 0.24-22.19, P=0.469), reported David Kaplan, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

However, "there is a suggestion that statins may actually reduce decompensation and liver cancer events, but further data will be needed," Kaplan told MedPage Today. What is clear is that statins are safe for patients with cirrhosis and shouldn't be withheld from those who have indications, he added.

"Our hope is that, with additional data from the Liver Cirrhosis Network's RESCU study of rosuvastatin, our data and their data together may be able to move the needle forward on statin initiation," Kaplan said.

Statins could provide anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic benefits while lowering hepatic portal vein pressure in cirrhosis. Observational studies have pointed to lower risks of decompensation and death, including research in veterans with hepatitis C-related compensated cirrhosis and a large study that was also presented at the Liver Meeting in patients with cirrhosis caused primarily by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, randomized trials have shown unfavorable results.

The SACRED trial was conducted at 11 VA medical centers and included patients with high-risk compensated cirrhosis caused by viral hepatitis, alcohol, and/or MASLD. High-risk factors included esophageal varices on endoscopy, portosystemic collaterals on imaging, a vibration-controlled transient elastography liver stiffness of at least 25 kPa, and platelets no greater than 70,000/mm3.

Participants couldn't have a standard indication for statins or statin exposure in the prior 6 months. That exclusion narrowed the study's size and power, Kaplan noted, given the "extremely high fraction" of those in the potentially eligible population who were either on statins or had well-established indications.

Median age was 60 years in the statin group and 64 years in the placebo group. Nearly all patients (93%) were men, and 73.9% were white. Cirrhosis etiology in the statin and placebo groups included alcohol (57.7% and 64.1%, respectively), hepatitis C (39.7% and 37.5%), and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (29.5% and 18.8%). The median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score in both groups was 14. About one-third of both groups were on a non-specific beta blocker (NSBB).

Roughly 40% of the study population had previously cured hepatitis C, Kaplan said, which may have lowered the study's overall event rate and made it more challenging to show a treatment difference.

Of note, HCC occurred in 2.56% of statin patients and 7.81% of placebo patients. HCC events showed the numerically largest difference between the statin and placebo groups, Kaplan noted. Ongoing chemoprevention studies could shed light on how statins might specifically impact liver cancer risk, he added.

The two groups' restricted mean survival times (RMST) showed an advantage with statin therapy. The statin group had an RMST of 702 days compared with the placebo group's 651 days -- a significant 51-day difference (P=0.043). Despite the significance, Kaplan cautioned, "I think one has to be somewhat conservative with the interpretation."

There was also a suggestion of benefit for the primary endpoint when a baseline NSBB was paired with a statin (HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02-1.19, P=0.071).

Adverse event rates were similar in the statin and placebo groups, at 94.9% and 93.8%, respectively. Serious adverse events occurred more frequently in the placebo group (45.3%) than the statin group (35.9%), as did liver-related events (6.3% vs 5.1%). Possible treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 1.6% of the placebo group and 2.6% of the statin group.

Study limitations included the small sample size and the low rates of endpoint events.

Applications that are selected to move on will be tasked with submitting a more fleshed-out proposal, including details on implementation, AI governance and sustainability.

CareSource is aiming to identify solutions that are ready for implementation and has the potential for scale. Potential focus areas include care coordination, member engagement, behavioral health and rural healthcare. Solutions should use AI to support care delivery, but it should not replace human judgement or oversight, the insurer said.

To be eligible, a qualified nonprofit organization must be leading the effort, according to the announcement. Technology companies, academic researchers, healthcare organizations and community-based groups can also play a role as partners.

#5667. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

#5665. Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation

Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."
