Fulton is credited with overseeing improved quality and financial stabilization during her time at the three-hospital nonprofit system.

> Tenet Healthcare Chief Information Officer Paola Arbour plans to retire at the end of this year, according to a recent regulatory filing from the for-profit hospital and ambulatory surgical center chain. She's been in the role since 2018, and plans to stick with the organization in a part-time, non-executive role through April 1, 2028 "to provide continuing transition services and support."

> Samuel Marchio was named senior vice president, chief government relations and policy officer at Ascension, per a social media post. He comes off a 15-year stint at Elevance Health (initially Anthem), where most recently served as regional vice president of federal government affairs.

> Stephen Taluja was named chief mission officer of Providence, a role that tasks him with aligning the Catholic nonprofit system's charity and service aims with ongoing strategic and organizational transformation. The appointment takes effect on June 29.

Taluja comes to the organization from a Bon Secours Mercy Health, where he is currently chief sponsorship and formation officer. He's been there in various roles since 2014, and before that led multicultural parish ministries.

> Addiction treatment provider Birches Health has added former Cigna Chief Medical Officer Doug Nemecek, M.D., to its advisory board as a senior adviser. As a senior adviser, Nemecek will work closely with the leadership team at Birches as it evolves its clinical and payer engagement strategies.

Nemecek's experience in the payer market will be key to informing this work, according to an announcement.

> Oraida Roman has been named as Aledade's new chief commercial officer, the company revealed on Wednesday. In the role, she will be tasked with leading the team's strategy around national health plan partnerships.

Roman brings 25 years of experience to the role, and will spearhead work around 200 contracts including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial plans.

> WellSpan Health President and CEO Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D, is calling it a career after more than eight years at the nonprofit system's helm.

WellSpan's board announced the plans April 6, sharing that Gapstur will continue in the role until the transition to a replacement is complete. No specific or expected timeline was given, other than sharing that a national search for that new executive has begun.

The system, which employs 23,000 people, has grown under her tenure from eight hospitals to 12, and from $2.5 billion of revenue to $4.7 billion. Its footprint has also expanded from five counties to 12 across Pennsylvania and northern Maryland, now reaching more than 1 million patients.

The announcement credits Gapstur with bringing "clear strategic direction" that focused on quality, safety, patient experience and employee engagement. That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two new positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The company said in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the company's Medicaid and commercial segments. He joins the insurer from Convey Health Solutions, where he was CEO, and has also previously served as president of Aetna at CVS Health.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the company as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

London said in the announcement that the shift recognizes Carson's significant contributions to the company and the experience that Finke brings to the table in driving operations forward.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

> Cory Mead was named CEO of HCA Florida Palms West Hospital, effective March 30. With more than a decade in leadership roles with HCA Healthcare, Mead most recently served as CEO of HCA Florida Woodmont Hospital.

> Elevance Health unveiled a slew of new leadership appointments within its Health Benefits business and Carelon, the unit leading services such as pharmacy benefits, behavioral health and value-based care enablement.

Kristy Duffey was named president of Carelon Health. The nurse practitioner-turned-executive recently helped scale care models and boost performance at Optum and CINQCARE. She'll be taking over for Peter Haytaian, who's slated to leave the role on May 4 to focus on family commitments but will remain through the end of the year as a special advisor to ease the transition, the company previously announced.

Aimée Dailey was appointed president of government business. She's already attributed with playing "a pivotal role" in expanding Elevance's government programs, and will now have responsibilities covering Medicare, Medicaid, Federal Government Solutions and Group Retiree Solutions.

Additionally, Will Feest, currently chief operating officer for Carelon, will be adding president of Carelon Insights to his title card; Darrell Oliveira was named chief financial officer for Carelon; and Jeff Plante, previously president of Carelon Insights, was dubbed chief financial officer for the Health Benefits segment.

Elevance said the new leaders will help expand and scale Carelon, which reaches over 90 million healthcare consumers. The Health Benefits segment provides coordinated solutions to more than 45 million Elevance members.

> Kurt Small was named president and CEO of CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield, effective May 4.

Small is currently president of Medicaid at Elevance Health, where he has been for nearly seven years. He has over 25 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, Highmark and Aetna.

At Elevance, he oversaw a Medicaid business with about 8.5 million members. CareFirst, meanwhile, is a nonprofit with 3.5 million members primarily living in the District of Columbia, Maryland and Northern Virginia. It has been without a permanent top executive since last September, with Ja'Ron Bridges serving as interim president and CEO.

> Barclay Berdan, CEO of Texas Health Resources, will retire in September after four decades at the 29-hospital nonprofit.

The executive stepped into his role in 2014, and was credited by the organization in its announcement release for guiding the system "through some of the most complex public health challenges in modern U.S. history while leading significant transformation across the organization’s clinical, digital and operational capabilities."

On deck is Winjie Miao, who is currently senior executive vice president and chief operating officer. She's set for a promotion to president on April 5, priming her to step in as CEO in September when Berdan steps away. Miao has been Texas Health Resources' chief operating officer since 2022, but first joined the organization in 2000.

> Elisabeth Armstrong is the new chief of staff at the National Institutes of Health Office of the Director, filling in the void left with Seana Cranston's resignation earlier in March.

Armstrong, who has a doctorate in bioethics, comes from the Food and Drug Administration, where she served as director of the Office of the Executive Secretariat. Prior to joining government, she conducted healthcare policy equity research for Raymond James & Associates’ Global Equities and Investment, advised and held various ethics positions at biotech and healthcare organizations and was a broadcast journalist, among other roles.

> Cigna Healthcare, the insurance arm of the Cigna Group, announced that it named Stanley Crittenden, M.D., as its new chief medical officer.

In the role, Crittenden will the lead the insurer's clinical operations, and will be tasked with partnering with other key leaders across the company to support the central goals of improving access and simplifying the healthcare journey for both patients and providers.

Crittenden brings years of experience in managed care, value-based care and population health to the role, Cigna said in an announcement. He most recently served as CMO at Quantum Health, and also held leadership roles at Evergreen Nephrology, Anthem and Humana.

Crittenden is also board certified in internal medicine and nephrology, Cigna said.

“I’m honored to join Cigna Healthcare at this important moment in its transformation toward making health care simpler, more personalized and more affordable,” said Crittenden in the announcement. “I am committed to fostering a collaborative and supportive environment, doing everything we can to improve the experience and outcomes of all those we serve.”

> John Haupert, president and CEO of Atlanta-based Grady Health System, will be handing the reins over to current Chief Operating Officer Anthony Saul at the end of this year.

Saul is immediately claiming the president title, and will shuffle into the top spot on Jan. 1, 2027. Haupert will stick around through 2027 in an advisory role to soften the transition, support philanthropic and capital fundraising and provide strategic guidance on a new $1+ billion medical campus the nonprofit also announced this week.

Haupert has headed Grady for the past 15 years. Saul has been around for seven, initially joining as chief financial officer.

> AI-powered prior authorization company Humata Health is bringing Liz Fowler, former director of the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), onto its board of directors.

The company said in an announcement that Fowler's experience at CMMI will support the team's efforts to accelerate Humata's mission to ensure patients get the care they need quickly. At CMMI, Fowler was tasked with rethinking reimbursement in Medicare and Medicaid to drive uptake of value-based care, providing critical insights she can bring to Humata.

#5605. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5604. Opinion: New organ donation rules are unfair to families

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Tucker is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University.

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.

Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.

Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.

Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.

I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.

The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.

That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.

In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.

These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.

The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.

To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.

Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.

In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.

No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.

I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.

These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.

Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.

First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.

Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.

Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.

The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.

The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.

Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.

In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.

Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

#5603. CNCF data shows cloud native is the on-ramp to AI, and maintainers are paying the price

The global population of cloud-native developers has topped 21 million, but the headcount tells only part of the story. Artificial intelligence is changing what those developers build and how open-source projects absorb their work.

Fresh research is putting numbers on that shift. The latest State of Cloud Native Development report from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData Ltd. counts more than 21 million practitioners, or 41% of developers worldwide. Yet that figure likely misses many people who rely on cloud-native infrastructure without knowing it, according to Bob Killen (pictured, right), director of technical program management at CNCF.

“The big thing is it actually might be undercounting a significant amount of them,” Killen said. “Because there’s a very large amount of people that are essentially consuming cloud-native applications without even realizing it.”

Killen and Liam Bollmann-Dodd (left), principal market research consultant at SlashData, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the latest State of Cloud Native Development findings, AI adoption, the strain on open-source maintainers and the shift toward cost discipline. (* Disclosure below.)

The report’s most striking finding concerns AI. About 75% of cloud-native developers use AI in some form, compared with only about 55% of other developers, Bollmann-Dodd noted. The gap mirrors a broader trend of agentic AI pushing Kubernetes into a second act.

“It’s a massive difference,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “So somehow being cloud native enables you and your organization and your personal stack to do AI in all its forms.”

The same AI wave is straining the people who keep the ecosystem running. Sustainability dominated the Maintainer Summit ahead of KubeCon, as maintainers face a flood of pull requests frequently generated by agents, Killen explained.

“How do we as maintainers keep up with the flooding of PRs and issues and things like that?” Killen said. “Especially when many of them are frankly just slop. And the real frustrating part is they’ll be just good enough.”

Cost discipline is the next shift. Just as financial operations practices followed rising cloud bills, cloud-native developers will soon manage model and token spending closely, according to Bollmann-Dodd.

“I think token maxing is dead and it’s going to stay dead forever,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “And I think it’s going to become much more focused on how you spend your money and how you spend your tokens.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA:

#5602. Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

Free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer. But new research suggests these often misunderstood molecules also play an important role in protecting us from the disease.

Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Even more surprisingly, tumors appear to exploit this requirement by releasing natural antioxidants that interfere with the immune system's ability to fight back.

The findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses. They could also point toward new strategies for making cancer immunotherapies more effective, particularly in patients whose tumors resist existing treatments.

How Cancer Uses Antioxidants to Disable Immune Cells

The immune system protects the body by identifying and eliminating threats, ranging from harmful bacteria and viruses to abnormal cells that can develop into cancer. Among its most important defenses are specialized immune cells called T cells, which can recognize and destroy tumor cells.

However, these cancer-fighting cells depend on chemical signals to activate their destructive abilities. Small amounts of reactive oxygen species provide some of those signals, helping T cells switch into attack mode.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom and Oregon Health & Science University in the United States discovered that tumors can interfere with this process. By examining the fluid surrounding cells inside tumors grown in mice, they found that cancer cells create chemical conditions that effectively prevent nearby T cells from activating.

The key is a naturally occurring antioxidant protein called Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1). Cancer cells release large quantities of this protein into their surroundings, where it removes the reactive oxygen species that T cells need to function. Without those activating signals, the immune cells become less effective at destroying cancer.

In effect, tumors use antioxidants as a chemical shield, weakening the immune response that would otherwise threaten their survival.

Removing Cancer's Antioxidant Shield Slows Tumor Growth

To investigate whether this defense mechanism could be disrupted, the researchers used CRISPR gene editing to modify cancer cells in mice. The edited cells could no longer produce PRDX1, allowing the team to examine what happened when tumors lost their ability to release the antioxidant protein.

The results were encouraging. Without PRDX1, immune cells became more active, and tumor growth was reduced. This suggested that interfering with the antioxidant protein could restore some of the immune system's ability to attack cancer.

The researchers then investigated whether human cancers use the same strategy. They examined existing data on proteins released by human cancer cell lines, studied patterns of gene activity in thousands of human tumors, and analyzed fluid collected from tumors surgically removed from patients.

All three lines of evidence supported the same conclusion. Human cancers also release PRDX1 into the surrounding environment, where it can eliminate the reactive oxygen species that cancer-fighting T cells rely on.

Dr. Xan Wesolowski, one of the lead authors from the University of Cambridge's Department of Pathology, explained why the discovery challenges conventional thinking about these molecules.

"We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding they have important functions within cells, and T cells need them to activate. Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination."

A New Strategy for Making Cancer Immunotherapy More Effective

Cancer treatment has increasingly focused on helping the immune system recognize and eliminate malignant cells. These approaches, known as immunotherapies, have produced remarkable results for some patients, but many others experience little or no benefit.

The new research identifies a possible reason certain tumors can withstand immune attacks. By releasing PRDX1, cancer cells may suppress the very T cells that immunotherapies are designed to activate.

Importantly, the researchers found that preventing cancer cells from producing this antioxidant improved their response to immunotherapy in experimental models. Some tumors that had previously resisted treatment became responsive when the antioxidant defense was disrupted.

Professor Rahul Roychoudhuri, also from Cambridge's Department of Pathology, said the findings identify a promising target for future cancer treatments.

"We've found a new way by which cancers shut down the immune system. When we block this process, tumors that don't respond to some immunotherapies start responding to treatment. That tells us this is a pathway worth targeting therapeutically, and there are several ways we might be able to achieve this."

The discovery also raises the possibility of using a different type of chemical approach to strengthen the immune response.

Dr. Robert Eil from the School of Medicine at Oregon Health & Science University said: "Our study suggests a possible way to boost T cell immunotherapies. Rather than using antioxidants, it could be that prooxidants can kickstart the T cells into action against tumor cells."

Why the Findings Raise Questions About Antioxidant Supplements

Beyond their potential implications for cancer treatment, the results may help explain a longstanding puzzle involving antioxidant supplements.

Antioxidants have frequently been promoted for their ability to neutralize reactive oxygen species and protect cells from damage. Because these molecules can contribute to processes associated with cancer development, researchers have investigated whether taking antioxidant supplements might reduce cancer risk.

However, several large randomized clinical trials have failed to demonstrate such protection. In some cases, antioxidant supplementation has even been associated with worse outcomes.

The new findings suggest one possible explanation. Although reactive oxygen species can damage cells, they also help activate the immune defenses that fight cancer. Removing too many of these molecules could unintentionally interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy tumors.

This does not establish that antioxidant supplements generally promote cancer, but it highlights the importance of understanding how these molecules behave in different biological settings.

The researchers also emphasize that their experimental findings remain preclinical. Although they identified evidence of the same antioxidant mechanism in human cancers, the potential treatment strategies have not yet been established as safe or effective in patients.

People living with cancer should therefore not change their diets, supplement use, or medical treatments based on these findings without consulting a healthcare professional.

The research was largely supported by the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council, Wellcome, and the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute.

#5600. Ardent Health acquiring Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47M

Ardent Health acquiring Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47M" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Ardent Health is acquiring Boone Health, a mid-sized nonprofit system based in Columbia, Missouri, for $47 million in cash, the organizations announced Thursday. It marks Ardent's first entry into the Missouri healthcare market.

The deal, expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, includes a 10-year, $200 million capital commitment on nonprofit Ardent’s part. That money will be invested in Boone’s facilities, workforce and, in the near term, an expansion of its emergency department, according to the announcement.

Ardent has agreed to maintain Boone’s essential hospital services while developing its 392-bed regional referral center, Boone Hospital Center. It also plans to maintain employment for existing Boone employees and providers, continue its charity care policy and establish a local advisory board.

“We are acquiring a strong asset in an attractive and growing midsize market with significant opportunity to drive operating and financial improvement, all while delivering high patient quality care and safety,” Ardent Health President and CEO Dave Caspers said during a Thursday afternoon investor call discussing the deal. “It also represents an effective use of capital at a compelling valuation that we expect will create long-term shareholder value.”

Alongside its main hospital, Ardent would acquire Boone’s medical group, 19 care sites including an outpatient campus and five medical office buildings, related ancillary services and real estate. The system is the second-largest provider in its region with about 30% market share and half a billion dollars of annual revenue, Caspers said, with a local population that is well insured (93% coverage) and growing well ahead of the national average (3.4% in the next five years).

“Boone expands our footprint into a new attractive market,” Caspers explained. “It diversifies our business and enhances scale. Further, adding Boone's regional system to our portfolio is consistent with our strategy of building leading healthcare platforms in growing mid-sized communities. We're highly aligned with Boone Health on culture and mission, including putting the patient at the center of everything we do, with an aim toward best-in-class clinical care, patient quality, safety and access to services.”

The executive noted to investors that Boone’s facilities are relatively modern and well maintained, allowing Ardent to direct more capital toward its growth. The company has also identified “meaningful opportunities to optimize financial performance.” By leveraging its larger scale and expertise to tackle costs (supply chain procurement, vendor consolidation) and revenue cycle processes, Ardent executives said they expect to generate about $5 million to $10 million additional EBITDA within the deal’s first year, and at least $30 million of annual synergies three years after the deal’s close.

Boone Health has been independent since 2021, following over three decades during which it operated as part of the BJC HealthCare system. In 2025, its leadership kicked off a search for potential strategic partners “that could provide additional capital and resources to support the system's continued growth. Ardent was selected after a comprehensive evaluation process led by an independent advisory firm,” according to Thursday’s announcement.

“In Ardent, we identified a partner that supports our mission, respects our culture and can accelerate our vision without compromising what makes Boone Health special,” Jerry Kennett, M.D., chair of Boone’s Board of Trustees, said in the announcement. "Following a thoughtful review, the Board is confident Ardent is the right long-term partner for Boone Health. This agreement protects what our community has built while giving Boone Health the resources it needs to grow."

Ardent Health’s current operations include 30 acute care hospitals and over 280 care sites, several of which are run as part of a joint venture structure with other health system partners. In 2025, the company increased its revenues by 6% to $6.3 billion and grew its adjusted EBITDA to $545 million.

The company recently logged a strong third quarter off the back of solid demand for emergent care and progress on its ongoing performance improvement initiative. In September, it also officially divested from a joint venture with the University of Kansas Health System, a decision that leadership said is part of an ongoing review of its portfolio to ensure long-term strategic fit among its hospitals and partnerships.

#5598. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#5596. Plan sponsor expectations, policy shifts set to pressure payers in 2027

Plan sponsor expectations, policy shifts set to pressure payers in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

2027 is shaping up to be a complex year for health plans, as demands from clients to demonstrate value get louder, according to a new report.

Analysts at consulting firm Numerof & Associates released their 2027 outlook report for the insurance industry, and said that in a world where the cost of healthcare continues to rise, more patients and plan sponsors are asking questions about what plans are bringing to the table.

Increasing transparency does make it easier for members to make their own healthcare decisions, but that alone isn't enough to resolve affordability challenges, per the report. It means that insurers will be tasked with engaging differently with consumers and transforming their experiences.

"The bigger issue is not just that healthcare costs keep rising but the traditional insurance model is becoming increasingly tough to sustain without demonstrating better value," said Michael Abrams, co-founder and managing partner at Numerof, in an interview. "Consumers and employers are getting more sensitized to the issue of value."

That interest in finding greater value is pushing employers to consider alternative models and approaches that can manage benefit costs, such as direct provider contracting, onsite clinics and care navigation programs.

The expectation is not just lower costs, but to drive better outcomes and have greater accountability over the medical benefit offerings, per the report. And this trend opens the door for new entrants to thrive, and challenge the role of health plans as the bridge between employers and providers.

Abrams said digital health companies that target certain specialty areas, such as musculoskeletal care or diabetes, have a significant opportunity to fill that gap.

"These digital healthcare companies aren’t necessarily replacing insurers; they’re competing for functions that insurers traditionally performed or should be performing," he said.

In addition, these trends are gaining steam at a time of significant policy upheaval, further complicating the outlook for health plans, according to the report. The expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act plans has driven up costs, and Medicaid work requirements taking effect on Jan. 1 could significantly grow the uninsured or underinsured population.

Reimbursement trends in other markets, such as Medicare Advantage, are also in the mix, the report said.

Abrams said the "convergence" of those policy changes with increased pressure from clients and members makes for a uniquely challenging combination.

"Insurers are getting squeezed from a number of different things all at the same time," he said.

The report recommends that plans looking to survive in this complex time should focus on demonstrating their value to plan sponsors and enrollees, particularly around managing the total cost of care. Insurers should also rethink how they engage with members to support a stronger relationship with consumers.

It also means finding ways to think differently about their relationship with providers; a step that will be critical to addressing the cost of care. Payers should look for provider partners that can take on risk, and work proactively with providers to drive better outcomes and improve value.

Abrams said that payer-provider dynamics are often coercive rather than collaborative. In one market, the insurer may be more powerful and in another the provider, but in either case it's based around a show of dominance rather than working together.

"With continued consolidation on both sides, we have seen a kind of polarization where the only mechanism for resolution is who has the biggest market clout," Abrams said.

#5595. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

#5593. CommonSpirit Health logs $544M operating loss to begin its FY2027

CommonSpirit Health logs $544M operating loss to begin its FY2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

CommonSpirit Health kicked off its 2027 fiscal year with a $544 million operating loss as decreasing acuity, dampening payer mix and other expenses outpaced the large nonprofit’s strong volumes and improving operating efficiency, according to financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

That operating loss excludes $65 million non-routine special charges incurred by the health system—most notably severance costs and other fees tied to its strategic, multi-billion-dollar decision to end a long-term revenue cycle contract with Tenet Healthcare—during the quarter, and reflect a -5.3% operating margin. The system had reported a $396 million operating loss and -4% margin during the same period a year prior.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) was $77 million in the quarter, also a dip from the prior year’s $129 million.

“Our first-quarter performance reflects steady operational progress, even amid persistent cost and reimbursement headwinds, as patients continue to choose CommonSpirit for quality care,” Chief Financial Officer Michael P. Browning said in a release.

CommonSpirit, already one of the country’s largest health systems, said it grew its quarterly operating revenue 5.3% year over year to $10.3 billion. The uptick included a 2.8% year-over-year increase in adjusted admissions as well as $165 million in net income from the California provider fee program, as opposed to no such benefit recorded the year prior. At the same time, the organization said its revenues were affected by “revenue yield challenges” and increases in self-pay, Medicare and Medicaid among its payer mix—both issues cited in recent financial reports from other major health systems.

Meanwhile, CommonSpirit’s operating expenses (before special charges) rose 6.6% year over year to nearly $10.9 billion. Much of the increase was tied to higher volumes as well as salary inflation, the latter of which came even as the organization improved its labor productivity (hospital full-time equivalents per adjusted admission decreased by 1.4%) and cut down its contract labor spend.

CommonSpirit’s results also included $115 million of net nonoperating income, substantially less than the year before due to “market fluctuations” affecting its investment returns. That left a bottom-line net loss of $496 million for the quarter and, as of Sept. 30, 160 days of cash on hand.

Management, in the filing and an accompanying press release, noted that the quarter’s numbers land as the system continues to execute on a sweeping operating performance improvement plan. That effort includes work to boost volumes through a focus on its care network, revenue realization efforts surrounding denials and managed care negotiations, standardizing department staffing models to trim labor costs and potential service line rationalization “for those markets where performance is currently below requirements.”

“We are making deliberate, near-term investments to unify our electronic health record, enterprise resource planning and revenue cycle platforms, while advancing responsible AI adoption to strengthen our system for the long term,” Browning said. “Keeping patients at the center of everything we do requires disciplined expense management and fair, timely reimbursement for the care we deliver.”

“Financial sustainability is what makes our mission possible,” added President and CEO Wright Lassiter III in the release. “Through disciplined operations, we are supporting our team members, strengthening our ministry and protecting access to compassionate, high-quality care across the communities we serve.”

CommonSpirit Health comprises about 2,600 care sites, including 132 hospitals, and more than 160,000 employees across 24 states. In the most recent fiscal year ended June 30, it reported $42.4 billion in total operating revenue and a $430 million operating loss (-1% operating margin) before special charges, an improvement from the prior fiscal year.

#5592. New addiction society guidance on medetomidine’s brutal withdrawal

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Clinicians first noticed medetomidine in the Philadelphia drug supply during the spring of 2024. There was a cluster of overdoses one weekend, leaving patients more sedated and with lower heart rates than normal after receiving the reversal medication naloxone.

It raised some red flags, but amid a constantly changing drug supply, not many. None of the patients died, and most went home from the hospital the same day. It wasn’t until autumn, when patients started coming in with excruciating withdrawal symptoms, that doctors knew something had dangerously shifted.

“It took a while for our patients to consistently have a supply that was exposing them to this enough so that when they stopped, they would rapidly develop withdrawal,” said Jeanmarie Perrone, an emergency medicine physician and director of the Penn Medicine Center for Addiction Medicine and Policy. “It’s the withdrawal that has caused so many problems.”

While clinicians in Pennsylvania and other hotspots are now familiar with the signs of medetomidine withdrawal, the American Society of Addiction Medicine this week released the first national guidance for recognizing and treating patients who have taken the sedative. Technically, the document consists of “considerations,” not guidelines, since researchers have not yet conducted larger studies that could validate the inferences clinicians are making on the ground.

If people are using medetomidine, it’s nearly always in combination with illicit opioids, experts say. That means naloxone should still be the first step if somebody appears to be overdosing. But it also means the patient may not be responsive even after they start breathing again. When it comes to acute medetomidine intoxication, low heart rate and low blood pressure can be treated with IV fluids and other basic care, the guidance notes.

The first symptoms of medetomidine withdrawal tend to be nausea and vomiting, without the diarrhea that accompanies opioid withdrawal, said Perrone, one of the co-authors. That’s when they recommend clonidine, a medication that, like medetomidine and xylazine before it, acts as an alpha-2 agonist. If that doesn’t help or patients can’t keep it down, they could develop very high blood pressure and a fast heart rate within a few hours. That may signal the need for the related IV medication dexmedetomidine, or Precedex.

“It’s scary. We thought we were already living in unprecedented times with the adulteration of fentanyl with xylazine,” said Kory London, an emergency physician and addiction specialist at Thomas Jefferson University. (He didn’t contribute to the considerations, but he works with many people who did.) Unlike withdrawal from other illicit drugs, coming off of medetomidine may require a stay in the intensive care unit.

“We are giving doses [of clonidine and dexmedetomidine] that, as an experienced addiction provider, I would not have given five years ago when dealing with the initial xylazine adulteration,” London said. “Unless you’re experienced with this, giving enough medications to avoid getting somebody to the ICU is really challenging.”

Before medetomidine started taking over, xylazine was the dominant adulterant in much of the American drug supply. It leaves users with horrific wounds and is such a powerful sedative that it could knock people out for hours, often leaving them vulnerable in public.

Medetomidine doesn’t seem to cause the same wounds. But as a sedative, it’s far more potent.

By the end of 2025, medetomidine had been detected in at least 18 states. It’s important for physicians to know whether medetomidine is present in the local drug supply, experts emphasize, as the symptoms may resemble other conditions, including sepsis. In general, it’s critical to stay familiar with the local supply and to consider what effects different adulterants could have on users, said Michael Lynch, a co-author of the considerations and an emergency medicine doctor specializing in medical toxicology at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.

“The next thing, and then the next thing, and then the thing after that are coming,” Lynch said. “We can try to predict what they’re going to be, but we can’t always.”

Not every community has the resources to do rigorous, regular drug checking. But “if we do a good job at describing our experience in places where we do have resources and have that early experience, hopefully other places can see the clinical manifestation,” Lynch said. There are drug testing strips for medetomidine.

While the clinical considerations offer doctors a blueprint for treating medetomidine withdrawal, experts say that more research is needed to understand the drug’s long-term effects and to develop better treatments.

Some patients who make it through withdrawal and begin to take medications for opioid use disorder can still experience cravings, experts said. They might think that the cravings are for opioids and begin to use again, but really, the cravings are for medetomidine.

“We’re going to have to recognize that there are now patients who are developing a sort of novel substance use disorder of alpha-2 agonist sedative addiction,” said London. “We urgently need both ways to understand that and ways potentially to help treat patients.”

#5591. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.
