#5574. Joanna Gaines Reveals How Her Approach to Holiday Decorating Has Evolved as She’s Gotten Older

Joanna Gaines keeps a beautifully decorated home year-round, so it’s no surprise that she pulls out all the stops for the holidays.

The “Fixer Upper” star recently shared her best holiday hosting tips as she prepares to celebrate the season with her family. She also noted the surprising way her approach has changed over time.

“The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” Gaines, 48, told USA Today. “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.”

While the Magnolia co-founder encouraged aspiring decorators to feel empowered to go big with their festive displays, she left room for those who prefer to take a more subdued route.

“There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.”

Gaines also noted that she’s committed to upholding food traditions, using recipes she’s been working on since she and Chip Gaines wed in 2003.

“Food is really at the center of our holidays,” she said. “Thanksgiving especially is this day I feel like I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.”

Gaines also detailed her approach to Christmas in the editor’s note she published in the Nov. 10 issue of Magnolia Journal.

“Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.”

She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory.

“Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.”

Explaining that she’s choosing to prioritize holding space for both the major moments and the much more relatable ones, Gaines also reflected on being the “gatekeeper” of her family’s yearly traditions as she aims to “do the same things” they always have, “if not bigger and better” this year.

She wrote about the “dressing up” that is encouraged toward the end of the year and romanticized the “fresh delight” of decorating the home, hosting loved ones, and “trying to create standout experiences” that her “kids will remember and tell their kids about someday.”

The Gaineses certainly have their hands full with their five children: Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8. But during a recent conversation on the “Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce” podcast, the proud mom revealed that they’d recently been discussing the idea of expanding the family once again.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

“He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” Gaines quipped, adding that her husband had even told their “grown kids” that she was expecting, and their eldest daughter said that she’s “not coming home” if the news is true.

The HGTV personality went on to encourage Kelce, a mom of four, to add another little one to her family.

“Five is a good number,” Gaines said, noting that she would “have more babies” if she “could.”

#5573. DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues

A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium during a shooting spree on Thursday, police said.

The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area.

Matt Wade Lambert, 55, a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life.

Lambert was suspected of going down to the luxury VIDA Fitness center housed inside the building, locating the building manager, identified las 46-year-old James Stuart, next to the treadmills and shooting him with a handgun from a point-blank range, DC Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, according to WUSA9.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gymgoer James Spellman told The Associated Press. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout in the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and an order to shelter in place in the area.

While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect.

During a press conference Thursday evening, Interim DC Police Chief Jeff Carroll said that Lambert then ran out of the gym, went up to his seventh-floor patio and opened fire from a rifle, striking two men and two women who were downstairs. Earlier reports said three of them were construction workers.

One of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he ended his own life with a shotgun blast.

When officers breached the door, they found all three firearms used during the shootings, along with containers of flammable liquid.

DC Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence."

Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025. In it he claimed that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage.

Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment.

According to the filing, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027.

Attorney Joel Braithewaite, who represented Lambert in the case, told NBC News that he spoke with him just yesterday or the day before and said that the 55-year-old was "in a good place" and about to start a new job on Monday.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5572. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5571. Rates Come Down Again but Remain Over 7%

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates eased again for the fourth-straight week but remain almost a full percentage point over last year at this time, a key reason buyers continue to hold back and why the market remains sluggish.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.11%, down seven bases points from  7.18% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.24% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.45%, down from 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.

At presstime, the average rate was back up to 7.42% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said that while rates are at their lowest level since late September, borrowing costs are still nearly a full percentage point higher than they were last year at this time.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines,” she said. “In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets. Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly even if rates move higher.”

Sturtevant noted that data on pending home sales suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the fourth quarter. “It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jiayi Xu added that the recent downtrend trend with rates could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%.

“The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike,” Xu said in a statement. “On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast.”

Xu also said today’s homebuyers are being squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, with inflation being the bigger long-term problem.

“High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.”

#5570. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5569. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. #5568. Cisco beats expectations, lifts guidance and forecasts AI infrastructure revenue to double in fiscal 2027

Shares of Cisco Systems Inc. were flat in late trading today after the networking infrastructure giant reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s expectations.

The company also raised its guidance for fiscal 2027, citing strong demand for artificial intelligence network infrastructure.

Cisco reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.40 per share, comfortably beating the Street’s target of $1.33 per share. Revenue for the quarter jumped 24% from the same period one year earlier, to $18.5 billion, ahead of the $18.1 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, Cisco’s net income rose to $4.6 billion, up from just $2.9 billion a year ago.

Although the stock was flat in extended trading, it’s still up 32% in the year to date, way ahead of the broader Nasdaq index, which has gained just 9% over the same stretch.

Cisco has been pushing to gain a foothold in the AI infrastructure buildout that’s dominating the technology industry these days after failing to capitalize on the generative AI boom in the early days. However, its push has come at a critical juncture, as investors have become increasingly concerned over the prospects of a slowdown in data center building following the Democratic party’s sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, there are growing fears about the impact rising borrowing costs will have on debt-fueled data center construction projects.

Still, Cisco Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) expressed confidence in the company’s ability to maintain its momentum. He told analysts on a conference call that we’re still in the “very early stages of a multiyear network supercycle.” He said he’s confident Cisco’s AI networking technology is strong enough to continue to capture a portion of the multibillion-dollar opportunity that presents.

“Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” Robbins added.

Cisco is also building out its software portfolio with new tools that can help businesses to build armies of autonomous AI agents that can perform work on behalf of humans. It also sells the security software necessary to protect those agents and their underlying infrastructure against cyberattacks.

The company said it’s increasing its AI infrastructure revenue forecast for the fiscal year to $9 billion, which would be more than double what it earned in fiscal 2026. According to Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson, the company is “unlocking significant operating leverage,” and this is what’s enabling it to grow its earnings “much faster” than its revenue.

Investors may still be worried about Cisco’s gross margins, though. This has been a concern for many companies, as the global shortage of memory chips has steadily increased the cost of the components that hardware makers need to build their data center infrastructure products.  Cisco’s gross margin of 65.6% in the quarter was in-line with the Street’s estimates, but down from 68.1% in the year-ago period.

TECHnalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the decline was unlikely to worry too many people, though. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” he said. He added that the company’s raised forecast and strong earnings and revenue was the main thing the market wanted to see.

For the current quarter, Cisco said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.34 and $1.36 per share on sales of $18 billion to $18.2 billion. That’s a strong forecast, with the Street looking for earnings of just $1.23 per share on revenue of $17.88 billion.

#5567. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5566. Inside Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio as the Nvidia CEO Resigns After Affair with Suspected Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned after having extramarital affairs with a business executive—Alice Huang, who the U.S. government has determined to be working with Chinese intelligence—and a Nvidia employee.

Finance chief Colette Kress will work as the interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent replacement, Nvidia said Thursday.

External and internal candidates will be considered as the company searches for a Jensen's successor.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world," the statement read. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

The news follows a Nov. 8 statement from Huang, who admitted to the affairs.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang stated in a previous message to the company. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

While the board of Nvidia claimed it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” an external counsel will be selected to investigate

The revelation, first reported by the New York Times, is expected to have an economic impact not only on Nvidia—whose stock price has already taken a hit—but on the artificial intelligence industry as a whole, given the chipmaker’s influence.

The company was the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence bom.

According to the New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent to ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Larry Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

However, he has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan in 1963, spent his early childhood in Thailand. He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to America to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school.

While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

As the future of Nvidia's stock remains unclear, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech tycoon's expansive property portfolio.

In 2017, the tech tycoon splashed over $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is tied to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell, of Marble Management, previously told the Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Of course, Huang is also neighbors with Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech mogul owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters, which is in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

#5565. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

Buyers rarely get low rates and strong negotiating power at the same time, and today’s market is handing you the leverage. Connect with a local real estate agent to find homes where sellers may be open to covering a rate buydown or closing costs, so you can see if today’s market can work for your budget.

#5563. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5562. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5561. Nearly Half of Gen Z Admit Skipping Rent or Mortgages Just To Fund Holiday Spending

The holiday season is an exciting time, but it can also be very expensive.

If you’re careless, festive gatherings, gifts, and travel may leave you in debt well into the new year.

A new survey by Accredited Debt Relief found that 67% of Gen Z have taken on or expect to take on holiday debt this year. And nearly 15% of Americans are still paying off last year’s holiday debt.

Furthermore, 46% of Gen Z respondents have delayed or skipped rent or mortgage payments to afford holiday spending, compared with 28% of millennials, 14% of Gen X, and 3% of baby boomers.

“Holiday spending should never come at the expense of someone's financial stability, but these findings show just how difficult it can be to balance financial responsibilities with the social expectations and pressure to create a memorable holiday," said Bobbi Rebell, chief financial education adviser at Accredited Debt Relief in San Diego.

"Making tough choices around spending may feel like you’re disappointing those you care about, but protecting your financial future needs to be non-negotiable."

If you’re worried about holiday debt or keeping up with housing expenses, a bit of planning, dedication, and creativity can help you enjoy the season without putting your finances on the line.

Experts agree that your rent or mortgage and related bills should always come first, before you spend money on holiday extras.

“I’ve spent a lot of time helping people who have struggled to keep their homes. And I’ve seen how hard it can be to recover once things get out of control and they start falling behind on mortgage payments,” says Casey Yontz, bankruptcy attorney at Yontz Law, PLLC in Phoenix.

One missed mortgage payment probably isn’t going to get you into foreclosure, but it can be the beginning of a snowball of serious delinquency.

And depending on the terms of your loan, you can incur late fees on your missed payment.

Once that payment is 30 days late, it could get reported to credit bureaus and take a serious toll on your credit score. If you continue to fall behind, foreclosure is a possibility.

“It’s true that under federal mortgage-servicing rules, foreclosure generally cannot begin until you are 120 days behind. But this doesn’t mean you should treat these 120 days as extra time to spend money on something else, like holiday gifts or travel,” Yontz explains.

According to Yontz, there’s no holiday present that’s worth putting your family's home at risk.

Howard Dvorkin, chairman at Debt.com in Fort Lauderdale, FL, shares those thoughts.

“What’s worse: Someone thinking you cheaped out on their holiday gift? Or sleeping outside? Financially speaking, housing must be your top priority. I’ve yet to meet a client’s friends and family who would want you to jeopardize your housing,” says Dvorkin.

If you're still paying for the 2025 holidays, putting 2026 holiday expenses on another credit card is not the solution.

“Holiday debt is an indicator that your holiday spending is beyond your budget, and might be a little bit out of control,” says Yontz.

Stop adding to it, and be honest with yourself about the math.

Look at your actual income versus expenses and debt numbers.

Ask yourself these questions: How much do I still owe? What’s the interest rate? How much can I afford to pay each month after paying my living expenses?

“Try to prioritize higher-interest card debt first. Pay more than the minimum payments, because making minimum payments on credit cards is like throwing buckets of water on a five-alarm fire,” say Yontz.

Dvorkin also recommends seeking professional help.

“Call a certified credit counselor and receive a free, in-depth debt analysis. With that in hand, you can consider all your options and make an informed choice,” explains Dvorkin.

Depending on your situation, a debt management program may make sense. It can reduce your total credit card payments by up to half without any long-term damage to your credit score.

“It can also lower your interest rate to 10% or less—sometimes even zero. You pay a fee for a professional to set this up, but those fees are dwarfed by how much you save,” Dvorkin adds.

Holiday spending should come out of whatever disposable income you have left after paying for your necessities like housing, gas, and groceries.

These tips can help you enjoy the holiday season while still keeping your finances in check:

You'll save more if you focus on what to buy than how you buy it. That’s why a holiday budget is so important.

“Nothing evokes images of Scrooge more than sitting down with pen and paper and listing everything you'll buy. But we don't live in 'A Christmas Carol.' We have the technology to make holiday budgeting a breeze. There’s no shortage of apps that act as busy little elves and do the work for you,” say Dvorkin.

Inviting family members over for a no-cost game night will be far more memorable than buying each of them a shiny, new gadget.

“I just lost my mom this spring, and I can guarantee you that no present could ever be better than more time with her. Presents don’t matter, people do, in my opinion," Yontz explains.

You’ll notice a lot of companies that will let you buy something for the holidays and pay for it over time, especially if you’re shopping online.

Unfortunately, they’re not making your purchase any cheaper. In fact, you will probably end up paying more with interest and fees.

“They tempt you, and you pay for it. Don’t fall down the buy now, pay later chimney of misfit payments,” says Yontz.

Train your brain to dislike overspending.

Do some research on how much you’re actually paying for credit card debt if you have it. Notice how much you’re paying in interest when you buy something.

“When I started doing this, I felt like I was being taken advantage of and that was enough for me to not want to use credit cards,” Yontz explains.

At the end of the day, the holidays should be something your family remembers fondly, not something you're still paying for next Christmas.

#5560. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. And that means less rushing, fewer last-minute surprises, and a better chance to make a great first impression when you're ready to sell.Thinking about selling in 2027? #5559. Applied Materials posts impressive 53% jump in revenue as it beats expectations again

Semiconductor industry giant Applied Materials Inc. chalked up another strong quarter as it continued to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom, delivering fourth-quarter results that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations on earnings and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share on revenue of $10.41 billion, up by an impressive 53% from a year earlier. The results were impressive, with analysts modeling earnings of just $4.06 per share on sales of $10.3 billion. Net income rose to $2.71 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same period one year ago.

Applied Materials is the world’s biggest supplier of the equipment used by semiconductor manufacturers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc., so its results are widely seen as a bellwether for the broader chipmaking industry. If Applied is growing, it means chipmakers are investing in their factories and presumably expecting to churn out more chips, driving growth in the industry. The company manufactures all sorts of machines to support different semiconductor manufacturing processes, catering to the most advanced silicon for AI workloads.

Chief Executive Gary Dickerson (pictured) said the company delivered record-breaking results in fiscal 2026, with full-year sales rising 21% from the prior year, to $34.31 billion. He also said the semiconductor systems business unit is on track to grow more than 40% in calendar 2026. “AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors and Applied has the most-enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing roadmap, putting us in a great position for multiyear revenue and profit growth,” he added.

Applied’s stock was under pressure earlier in the day following the news of Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which came after he admitted to having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working for China’s intelligence services. Some investors worry that instability at Nvidia, which is the world’s most dominant AI chip supplier, could have a knock-on effect on the broader chipmaking industry.

However, the strong results brought Applied’s daytime slide to a halt, and the stock gained more than 2.5% in late trading. In the year to date, its stock is up 48%.

Applied’s main business, the semiconductor systems unit, saw revenue jump from $4.88 billion in the year-ago period to $7.99 billion. Meanwhile, sales from the smaller applied global services segment rose from $1.5 billion a year earlier, to $1.89 billion.

For the current quarter, Applied said it’s looking for earnings of $4.35 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue coming to $11.1 billion. Those numbers were better than expected too, with the Street modeling first quarter earnings of just $4.24 per share on sales of $10.85 billion.

During the quarter, Applied made a big splash when it said it’s going to invest $5 billion in a new chip research and development facility located in Silicon Valley. It’s called the EPIC Center, and it will act as a shared R&D center for chipmakers to collaborate on new process manufacturing technologies.

Initial partners include Intel Corp., which is working with Applied and other companies on the development of next-generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging technologies. Other founding partners include Kioxia Corp., BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. and the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.

“I’m incredibly excited to join the number one brokerage in East Tennessee,” Lewis added. “What really attracted me to REA is the opportunity to work with a company that understands the value of investing in its people. REA has created an environment where that kind of work is valued, and I’m excited to be part of it.”

“At REA, we believe our agents are our customers. Our responsibility is to create an environment where they can build successful, sustainable businesses and feel supported along the way. #5557. Khloé Kardashian Says Lamar Odom Is ‘Dead’ to Her After His Comments About Marrying for Family’s ‘Lifestyle’—Inside Their Former Marital Mansion

Khloé Kardashian is drawing a line through her relationship with her ex-husband, Lamar Odom.

On the Nov. 11 episode of “The Kardashians,” Kardashian got candid about what the former NBA star  said regarding their marriage in the Netflix documentary "Untold: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom."

“I did watch the Lamar documentary. I’m not too thrilled about it,” she said.

The mom of two, who was involved in the making of the documentary, previously expressed her “regret” in doing so on the April 15 episode of her podcast, “Khloé in Wonder Land.”

“I’m watching the documentary, and I’m like, 'Wait, I took time out of my life to sit here and do a favor for you,'” she continued on the family’s reality show. “I’m not being paid. I’m doing this ‘cause I’m trying to be nice.”

Kardashian found “many things” Odom said in the documentary to be “really distasteful.”

“You’re saying that you weren’t really in love with me, you married me just so you could be more popular in pop culture, all these things, which is so weird,” she explained. “Even if that is your truth, why don’t you say it without me being on the other side of these interviews? I just thought that was really, really lame.”

In the documentary, Odom said he found the Kardashian family’s “lifestyle” to be enticing. The couple married in 2009 just 30 days after meeting.

According to comments Odom’s friend Anthony “Pumpkin” Booker made in the documentary, on the day of the former couple’s wedding, the basketball player said he was “doing it to try to better his future” because the family had “mad connections.”

The Good American co-founder didn’t hold back when speaking about where she stands with Odom today.

“The bridge is burned, and there’s no more rope left to throw over. So he is dead to me,” she said. “This just solidifies what liars, con artists, cheats, thieves, trolls that men are. I just don’t want to be involved. Play with yourself, don’t play with me.”

Odom and Kardashian filed for divorce in 2013, citing “irreconcilable differences.” It was not finalized until 2016, as Odom had a near-fatal overdose in October 2015, prompting Kardashian to put the legal process on pause.

“He OD’d during the divorce, and I was his next of kin, even though it was still, the divorce was still—it was on the judge’s desk,” she said during a 2019 podcast appearance. “It was like, two years, or like a year or two of us trying to get the divorce going, and then this happened.”

She explained that the pause was “not for any romantic reasons.” It was so she could continue to “help take care of him and make sure that he would be OK again.”

After the split, it was reported that Kardashian kept the couple’s marital mansion, which was located in an upscale guard-gated community called Mulholland Estates in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Tarzana.

The former couple purchased the home for $3.95 million in December 2009, about two months after their wedding day.

The six-bedroom, 8.5-bathroom, Mediterranean mansion was heavily featured on both “Keeping Up With the Kardashians” and their spinoff, “Khloé and Lamar.”

All six of the en suite bathrooms were embellished with designer wallpaper, tumbled stone, mosaic accents, and custom closets. The primary suite also had a spalike bathroom and boasted expansive views of the city.

The 8,400-square-foot estate was equipped with all of the amenities you’d expect from a home of an NBA pro and a Kardashian: a home gym, a library, an office, and a theater room, among other luxuries.

Outside, a resort-like pool included stunning water features and was accompanied by fire pits and a spa.

The home was sold for $5.49 million in January 2014, with “The Big Bang Theory” star Kaley Cuoco snapping it up for nearly $1.5 million over the asking price.

Mulholland Estates wasn’t the only place Odom and Kardashian called home during their marriage. After Odom was traded to the Dallas Mavericks in 2012, they rented a posh condo at W Dallas Victory Hotel and Residences.

The $7,500-a-month dwelling had two bedrooms and two bathrooms and featured slate flooring, a wet bar, and bathrooms tiled with mother of pearl.

The building had amenities that included two fitness centers, a spa, an entertainment room, and a zero-edge infinity pool.

Following her separation from Odom, Kardashian purchased a $7.2 million Calabasas home in June 2014. The 9,214-square-foot estate was the former home of Justin Bieber.

Today, Kardashian lives in a stunning $17 million custom-built abode in Hidden Hills, CA, with the two children she shares with ex-boyfriend Tristan Thompson. The property is located right next door to her mother, Kris Jenner.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5556. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.
